domains.summary: Beyond the basics: migration strategies (the 6 R's), the Cloud Adoption Framework, TCO analysis, landing zones, and phased migration planning. Vendor-neutral study aid. Not affiliated with AWS; this course confers no certification.

scenarios.title: The Six R's
scenarios.situation: A company inventories 300 on-prem apps for migration. The portfolio includes: a stable legacy ERP nobody dares touch, a web app that could use managed database, a duplicate tooling app, and an old reporting server unused for a year.
scenarios.prompt: How should each be dispositioned under the 6 R's?
evidence: Rehost (lift-and-shift): move as-is. Replatform: minor optimizations (e.g., managed DB). Repurchase: move to SaaS. Refactor: re-architect for cloud-native. Retain: keep on-prem (for now). Retire: decommission.
choices: ERP: retain (too risky to move now); web app: replatform onto RDS; duplicate tooling: retire or repurchase as SaaS; unused reporting server: retire.
Rehost everything identically; disposition debates waste time.
Refactor all 300 apps to microservices for maximum cloud benefit.
Retire the ERP since it's old, and rehost the unused reporting server just in case.
scenarios.why: The R's are a triage tool: each app gets the least-disruptive strategy that captures available value — retain what can't move safely, replatform where managed services help, retire what's dead weight. Blanket rehosting imports all on-prem waste; blanket refactoring is a multi-year rewrite disguised as a migration.
scenarios.hint: Which app earns its migration cost, and which earns nothing at all?

scenarios.title: CAF Perspectives
scenarios.situation: A migration steering committee argues over who owns what: the CFO wants business-value tracking, HR worries about skills gaps, and security demands guardrails before any workload moves.
scenarios.prompt: How does the Cloud Adoption Framework assign these concerns?
evidence: Six perspectives: Business (value, outcomes), People (roles, skills, training), Governance (oversight, compliance), Platform (infrastructure, landing zone), Security (controls, identity), Operations (runbooks, monitoring). Each has capability owners.
choices: Business perspective: CFO's value tracking; People perspective: HR's skills plan; Security perspective: guardrails as a prerequisite; Governance ties them together with oversight.
All concerns belong to the Platform perspective since it's all infrastructure anyway.
Security owns everything; other perspectives are optional documentation.
Skip CAF — frameworks slow down migrations that just need engineers.
scenarios.why: CAF's value is making implicit ownership explicit: each perspective names capabilities and owners so value tracking, skills, and guardrails all have a home instead of falling between teams. Collapsing everything into 'infrastructure' is how skills gaps and missing guardrails become migration surprises.
scenarios.hint: If nobody owns the skills gap, when does it get discovered?

scenarios.title: TCO Showdown
scenarios.situation: The CFO compares 3-year on-prem refresh ($2M servers + facilities) against AWS estimates. The AWS estimate only counts EC2 hours and looks dramatically cheaper. The infrastructure team is skeptical.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a fair TCO comparison?
evidence: Total Cost of Ownership: on-prem includes hardware, power, cooling, space, network, staff time, refresh cycles, and downtime risk. Cloud includes compute, storage, transfer, support, and the migration itself. AWS's TCO calculators model both sides; hidden costs on either side invalidate the comparison.
choices: Count everything on both sides: on-prem power/cooling/space/staff/refresh plus cloud data transfer, support, storage growth, and migration cost — then compare over the same horizon with the same assumptions.
Accept the EC2-hours estimate; it's the biggest line item so it's close enough.
Add 50% to the AWS number as a safety margin and call it analysis.
Compare only year-one costs; beyond that both sides are guesses anyway.
scenarios.why: TCO comparisons fail on omitted costs, not on arithmetic: on-prem hides facilities and staff time, cloud hides transfer and growth — and the migration itself is a real cost. Same horizon, same assumptions, all line items, or the 'savings' are fiction either side can manufacture.
scenarios.hint: Which costs disappear from each column when they're inconvenient?

scenarios.title: Landing Zone First
scenarios.situation: A team migrates its first production workload into a single AWS account created with a personal email, no SSO, and the root user doing daily work. The second workload is starting next month.
scenarios.prompt: What should have been built before workload one?
evidence: A landing zone is the pre-configured multi-account foundation: AWS Organizations with OUs (security, infrastructure, workloads), SSO/Identity Center for human access, centralized logging (CloudTrail/Config), SCP guardrails, and network baselines — often via Control Tower.
choices: A landing zone: Organizations with separate accounts per workload/environment, Identity Center SSO (no daily root use), centralized logging, and SCP guardrails — built before the first production workload, not after the fifth.
More EC2 instances; the account structure can be sorted out during the next audit.
One shared admin IAM user per team as a compromise between root and SSO.
Separate VPCs in the same account; accounts are just billing constructs.
scenarios.why: Account structure is the security and blast-radius boundary: retrofitting multi-account, SSO, and centralized logging under live production workloads is surgery, while building it first is setup. Shared credentials and daily root use are the findings auditors write up first.
scenarios.hint: How do you un-share a root credential after a year of daily use?

scenarios.title: Wave Planning
scenarios.situation: With 300 apps to migrate, leadership wants 'everything by Q2.' The discovery data shows deep dependencies: the billing system touches 40 other apps, and nobody knows which servers the warehouse app needs.
scenarios.prompt: How should migration waves be sequenced?
evidence: Application Discovery Service maps dependencies. Migrate in waves: low-risk, low-dependency apps first to build muscle; dependency-heavy core systems later with their dependents grouped; each wave has rollback criteria and a pilot cohort.
choices: Sequence by dependency mapping: pilot wave of simple, low-dependency apps to prove the factory, then waves grouped by dependency clusters (billing with its 40 dependents together), core systems last with explicit rollback criteria.
Migrate alphabetically; fairness demands equal treatment.
Start with the billing system — biggest value first, dependencies can be discovered during cutover.
Move everything in one big-bang weekend; waves just prolong the pain.
scenarios.why: Dependencies dictate order: migrating a system without its dependents (or vice versa) breaks integrations at cutover, while a pilot wave de-risks the process on forgiving workloads. Big-bang migrations concentrate all risk into one unrecoverable weekend; alphabetical order ignores reality entirely.
scenarios.hint: What breaks if billing moves but its 40 dependents don't?

scenarios.title: The Refactor Bet
scenarios.situation: A monolithic order system is proposed for rehosting as-is. An architect argues for re-architecting to microservices on ECS with event-driven order flow — 9 months of work before any migration value.
scenarios.prompt: When does the refactor bet pay off, and what's the safer path?
evidence: Rehost captures migration speed; refactor captures cloud-native value (elasticity, resilience, deployment velocity) at high upfront cost and risk. The strangler fig pattern incrementally replaces monolith pieces behind the same interface, de-risking the rewrite.
choices: Rehost first to capture migration value and learn the platform, then strangler-fig the highest-value seams (order flow) toward events/microservices — refactor where the business case is proven, not as a big-bang prerequisite.
Refactor everything before migrating; a monolith in the cloud is a failure.
Rehost and declare victory; architecture never needs to change again.
Rewrite in a new language simultaneously — if you're refactoring, go all the way.
scenarios.why: The refactor bet pays when specific pain (scaling limits, deploy fear, outage blast radius) has a price tag exceeding the rewrite cost — which is rarely 'the whole monolith on day one.' Strangler-fig sequencing earns migration value immediately while retiring the riskiest seams first; big-bang rewrites combine migration risk with rewrite risk.
scenarios.hint: What exactly is painful about the monolith today — and what would fix only that?

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Aws Cloud Practitioner Plus as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy failure in Aws Cloud Practitioner Plus.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy
evidence: All Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Navigate the Bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You have 30 days before your assessment. You open the bootcamp and see 15 domains, a terminal, drills, and a mock. You feel overwhelmed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first week plan?
choices: Complete Start Here, then work the first three core domains in order — lessons with knowledge checks, then their scenarios, then one lab. Establish the daily loop before widening.
Take the full mock on day one to 'see where you stand,' then study randomly.
Read every lesson in all 15 domains first, then attempt scenarios in week three.
Skip lessons entirely and grind drills — speed matters more than understanding.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is the structured loop: Start Here orients you, then sequential domains build the foundation scenarios assume. The mock on day one wastes your only baseline and demoralizes; random study leaves gaps the assessment will find. Drills without understanding produce fast wrong answers.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the scenarios assume you already know.
evidence: 30 days available, ~2 hours per day on weekdays

scenarios.title: When You Get Stuck
scenarios.situation: You have failed the same scenario three times. The explanation makes sense when you read it, but you keep choosing wrong under time pressure.
choices: Drop back to the lesson: re-read the concepts, write out the decision process in your own words, then re-attempt the scenario untimed before going timed again.
Keep re-attempting the scenario until you memorize the right answer.
Skip it and move on — one scenario will not decide the assessment.
Look up the answer online and move faster through the rest.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats repeated failure as a signal: the mental model is broken, not the memory. Rebuilding from the lesson concepts — in your own words — repairs the model. Memorizing the answer passes one scenario and fails the next variation. The assessment tests patterns, not instances.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem memory or the underlying mental model?
objectives: Repair mental models from lesson concepts
evidence: Scenario failed 3x: same wrong choice twice, different wrong choice once

domains.name: IAM and Access Management

scenarios.title: The Leaked Access Key
scenarios.situation: An engineer accidentally pushed an AWS access key to a public GitHub repo. The key belongs to a deployment IAM user with broad permissions.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct immediate response?
choices: Immediately deactivate/delete the key, review CloudTrail for misuse during the exposure window, rotate any exposed secrets, then replace the long-term key with a role-based deployment (OIDC) so the key class disappears.
Change the GitHub password.
Rotate the key next sprint — it is probably fine.
Delete the repo and hope nobody saw it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats exposure as compromise: kill the key first, then investigate the window via CloudTrail, then eliminate the key class with OIDC federation for deployments. Waiting a sprint leaves the window open; deleting the repo does not recall the key; the GitHub password is irrelevant to the exposed credential.
scenarios.hint: Assume the key is already in an attacker's database. What limits the damage?
evidence: Key committed 6 hours ago; repo has 40 stars

scenarios.title: The Mysterious AccessDenied
scenarios.situation: A developer's IAM user has an Allow for s3:GetObject on the bucket, but every request returns AccessDenied. The policy looks correct.
choices: S3 must be down.
An explicit Deny somewhere in the evaluation chain: another attached policy, a permission boundary, or an SCP on the account — Deny always overrides Allow.
The bucket must be in the wrong region.
The developer needs AdministratorAccess temporarily.
scenarios.why: The correct approach follows evaluation logic: Allow is necessary but not sufficient — any explicit Deny (identity policy, boundary, or SCP) vetoes it. The Policy Simulator shows the deciding statement. Region and outages do not produce AccessDenied; AdministratorAccess is never the diagnostic step.
scenarios.hint: What beats an Allow in the evaluation logic?
evidence: Allow s3:GetObject present; SCP denies s3:* except from approved roles

scenarios.title: The Partner Account
scenarios.situation: A partner company needs read access to one S3 bucket in your account for 30 days. They have their own AWS account.
choices: Make the bucket public for 30 days.
Give them your account's root credentials temporarily.

Create a cross-account IAM role with a trust policy for the partner's account ID (plus ExternalId), granting s3:GetObject on that bucket only. They assume the role — no long-term keys cross the boundary.
Create an IAM user for the partner and email them the access key.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses temporary credentials across the trust boundary: the role's trust policy names the partner account, ExternalId prevents the confused-deputy problem, and the permission policy scopes to one bucket. IAM users for outsiders create offboarding debt; public buckets and shared root are non-starters.
scenarios.hint: How do you grant access that automatically expires without a key to rotate?
evidence: Partner account 999888777666; read-only; 30 days; one bucket

scenarios.title: The Stolen Password
scenarios.situation: An admin's console password was phished. The account has no MFA. CloudTrail shows the attacker listed S3 buckets but nothing else — yet.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do right now?
choices: Delete the admin user.
Wait to see if data is exfiltrated.
Force a password reset and move on.
Immediately revoke the admin's sessions and keys, rotate the password, enable MFA, attach the MFA-enforcement Deny policy, and scope the incident in CloudTrail — then require MFA org-wide.
scenarios.why: The correct approach contains first: revoke sessions and keys to cut access, then remediate (MFA everywhere, enforcement policy), then scope via CloudTrail. A password reset alone leaves active sessions; deleting the user destroys the audit trail; waiting surrenders the window the attacker already has.
scenarios.hint: What access does the attacker still hold while you deliberate?
evidence: ConsoleLogin success from new IP; ListBuckets x40; no data-plane calls yet

scenarios.title: The 200-Person Onboarding
scenarios.situation: Your company (200 engineers, Okta as IdP, 15 AWS accounts) onboards AWS access. Someone proposes creating IAM users in each account.
choices: Federate via IAM Identity Center with Okta (SAML): define permission sets once, assign to Okta groups per account. Engineers get portal login with short-term credentials — no long-term keys, offboarding in one place.
Give everyone the root credentials in a shared vault.
IAM users per account — it is simple and explicit.
One shared IAM user per team to reduce count.
scenarios.why: The correct approach eliminates the key class at scale: federation means joiners/leavers are IdP group changes, permission sets keep access consistent across 15 accounts, and there are no access keys to rotate or leak. Per-account IAM users create 3000 identities to manage; shared users destroy auditability.
scenarios.hint: What happens on an employee's last day under each design?
evidence: 200 engineers; Okta IdP; 15 accounts; high contractor churn

scenarios.title: The Delegated Administrators
scenarios.situation: Team leads need to create IAM roles for their teams, but must never be able to grant admin-level or cross-team permissions.
choices: Trust the team leads — they are senior.
A permission boundary on the team leads' admin role: it caps the maximum permissions any role they create can ever have, even if they attach AdministratorAccess — the boundary vetoes it.
A weekly manual audit of created roles.
Deny them iam:* entirely.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses the guardrail built for delegation: permission boundaries cap effective permissions regardless of attached policies, so leads stay productive within a blast radius you define. Trust is not a control; weekly audits catch damage after the fact; denying iam:* removes the delegation you wanted.
scenarios.hint: What caps permissions even when the attached policy allows more?
evidence: Leads create team roles; must be unable to self-escalate to admin

scenarios.title: The Root Audit
scenarios.situation: An auditor asks: how is the organization's root user protected, and how would you know if it were used?
choices: Root has MFA enabled, no access keys exist for it, it is locked away with break-glass documentation, and CloudTrail has an alarm on every root login — any use pages security immediately.
We deleted the root user.
Root is only used for billing.
The root password is strong — that is sufficient.
scenarios.why: The correct approach covers all four controls: MFA on the credential, no keys (the highest-risk form), procedural lock-away with documented break-glass, and detective control (CloudTrail alarm on root usage — root should never log in). A strong password alone is one factor; root cannot be deleted, only secured.
scenarios.hint: Root login should be an event that never happens. How do you guarantee you hear about it?
evidence: Show root MFA status, key inventory, and root-usage alerting

domains.name: Compute Services

scenarios.title: The Viral Spike
scenarios.situation: Marketing's campaign goes viral: traffic jumps 10x for 3 hours, then returns to normal. The app runs on two fixed EC2 instances.
choices: Move everything to the largest instance type available.
Turn off the instances during the spike to save money.
Add 20 On-Demand instances permanently — safe and simple.

Put the fleet in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB with target-tracking scaling: base capacity on On-Demand or Savings Plans, burst on Spot. Scales up for the spike, back down after — you pay for the 3 hours, not forever.
scenarios.why: The correct approach scales with demand: target tracking adds capacity as traffic rises and removes it after, while the ALB spreads load and health-checks. Mixed pricing (steady base + Spot burst) minimizes cost. Permanent instances pay for idle; bigger instances do not scale; turning off during peak is self-sabotage.
scenarios.hint: What should capacity do when the spike ends?
evidence: Baseline 200 rps; spike 2,100 rps for 3h; then baseline

scenarios.title: The Nightly Batch
scenarios.situation: A video-render batch runs 4 hours nightly. It checkpoints progress every 10 minutes and tolerates restarts. Currently on On-Demand.
scenarios.prompt: What is the cheapest correct compute?
choices: EC2 Spot (or Fargate Spot): up to 90% off; interruptions are fine because the job checkpoints and restarts. The workload's fault tolerance is what makes Spot safe.
Lambda with 15-minute chunks stitched together.
On-Demand — batch jobs need stability.
Dedicated Hosts for compliance.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches pricing to fault tolerance: checkpointed, restartable batch work is the textbook Spot case. On-Demand pays full price for tolerance you do not need; Dedicated Hosts solve a compliance problem you do not have; Lambda stitching adds complexity for no benefit.
scenarios.hint: What happens if the instance is interrupted at minute 37?
evidence: 4h render; checkpoints every 10 min; restarts cleanly

scenarios.title: The 20-Minute Function
scenarios.situation: A Lambda function processes large uploads but times out — the job needs 20 minutes. The team proposes chaining Lambdas.
choices: Split the upload into smaller files.
Move the job to Fargate or EC2: Lambda's 15-minute limit is architectural, not tunable. Chaining adds failure modes to dodge a limit that signals the wrong service.
Chain 2 Lambdas with Step Functions.
Increase memory to 10GB — more CPU means faster completion.
scenarios.why: The correct approach respects service boundaries: Lambda is for short, event-driven work; a 20-minute job is a container/VM workload. Step Function chains work but add orchestration complexity to avoid admitting the service mismatch. Memory helps marginally; splitting files does not change the job's nature.
scenarios.hint: Is the 15-minute limit tunable?
evidence: Timeout 15 min hit at 100%; job needs ~20 min

scenarios.title: The K8s Question
scenarios.situation: The team knows Docker but has no Kubernetes experience. They need to run one containerized API with 3 replicas, a load balancer, and deploys.
choices: EKS — Kubernetes is the industry standard.
Self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 for control.
ECS on Fargate: services, load balancer integration, and rolling deploys with no cluster to manage and no K8s learning curve. EKS pays off with K8s expertise or complex needs — not here.
One big EC2 instance with docker-compose.
scenarios.why: The correct approach picks the simplest tool that meets the need: ECS on Fargate gives replicas, ALB, and deploys without operating Kubernetes. EKS without K8s expertise is months of yak-shaving; self-managed K8s is worse; docker-compose on one box has no HA story.
scenarios.hint: What does the team actually need — containers running, or Kubernetes?
evidence: Docker-proficient; zero K8s experience; one API service

scenarios.title: The Startup MVP
scenarios.situation: A 3-person startup needs a standard Python web app in production next week: load-balanced, multi-AZ, with a database. No ops hire.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest sound choice?
choices: EKS with a service mesh.
A single EC2 instance — deal with HA later.
Hand-build a VPC, EC2 fleet, ALB, and RDS over two weeks.
Elastic Beanstalk: upload the code, get a load-balanced multi-AZ environment with managed updates. It trades some control for speed — exactly the right trade for an MVP with no ops team.
scenarios.why: The correct approach buys speed where it matters: Beanstalk provisions the load balancer, instances, and database from a code upload, with rolling deploys built in. Hand-building takes the two weeks you do not have; EKS is overkill; a single instance is a 3 AM pager waiting to happen.
scenarios.hint: What is the scarcest resource — control, or time?
evidence: 3 people; 1 week; standard web app; no ops

scenarios.title: The Game Server
scenarios.situation: A multiplayer game server needs UDP, 100k concurrent connections, static IPs for firewall allowlisting, and the lowest possible latency.
choices: NLB: TCP/UDP support, static IPs (Elastic IPs per AZ), ultra-low latency, millions of requests per second. ALB is HTTP-only — it cannot do UDP game traffic.
Route 53 DNS round-robin only.
ALB — it is the default.
Classic Load Balancer for simplicity.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches protocol and requirements: NLB handles UDP, provides static IPs for allowlists, and adds negligible latency. ALB cannot speak UDP at all; Classic is legacy; DNS round-robin has no health checking or connection-level balancing.
scenarios.hint: What protocol does the game speak?
evidence: UDP; 100k concurrent; static IPs; sub-10ms added latency

scenarios.title: The Flapping Fleet
scenarios.situation: An Auto Scaling group keeps terminating and replacing instances that are actually serving traffic fine. The cycle never stops.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: The AZs are unhealthy.

The health check is wrong: it probably hits a heavy endpoint (homepage with DB queries) with too-short timeouts, so slow-but-healthy instances get marked unhealthy. Fix with a lightweight /health endpoint and sane thresholds.
The instances are too small.
Auto Scaling is broken — use fixed instances.
scenarios.why: The correct approach suspects the measurement, not the instances: a health check that depends on the database or has aggressive timeouts will flap under load, and the ASG dutifully replaces victims. Right-sizing does not fix a bad probe; abandoning Auto Scaling surrenders elasticity; AZ blame needs evidence.
scenarios.hint: Who decides an instance is unhealthy — and what are they checking?
evidence: Replace cycle every 6 min; app logs show 200s on /health; /homepage p99 4s

domains.name: Storage Services

scenarios.title: The Forgotten Backups
scenarios.situation: Monthly S3 bill: $4,200. Analysis shows 80% is 3-year-old backups in Standard that are never read but must be retained 7 years for compliance.
choices: Move them to S3 Glacier Deep Archive via a lifecycle policy: ~$1/TB-month vs ~$23 for Standard. Retrieval takes hours, which is fine for compliance restores.
Move them to Standard-IA.
Buy more Standard storage.
Delete the backups — compliance is probably flexible.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches the access pattern to the cheapest tier that satisfies it: never-read compliance data is the textbook Deep Archive case, and lifecycle policies automate it. Deleting violates compliance; Standard-IA is still 20x the price for data never read; buying more of the wrong tier is not a strategy.
scenarios.hint: When was the last time anyone read these backups?
evidence: 38TB in Standard, 0 GETs in 12 months, 7-year retention required

scenarios.title: The Public Bucket
scenarios.situation: Access Analyzer flags a bucket as publicly readable. It hosts the company logo for the website.
choices: Make the whole bucket private and break the website.
Serve through CloudFront with Origin Access Control: the bucket stays private, CloudFront serves the logo publicly with caching. Verify no other objects are exposed; keep Block Public Access on.
Delete the bucket.
Leave it — the logo is meant to be public.
scenarios.why: The correct approach keeps the bucket private while serving public content properly: CloudFront with OAC is the designed pattern — private origin, public edge, plus caching. Leaving it public invites the next misconfigured object to be public too; breaking the site or deleting the bucket are not fixes.
scenarios.hint: Does the bucket need to be public, or just the logo reachable?
evidence: s3://assets allows public read; contains logo.png + 200 other objects

scenarios.title: The Ransomware Scare
scenarios.situation: A compromised admin credential deleted critical S3 objects. The bucket had no versioning. Leadership asks how to make this unrepeatable.
choices: Back up to the admin's laptop.
Nothing — the attacker is gone.

Enable versioning plus MFA Delete on critical buckets, enforce MFA via IAM policy, restrict delete permissions, and add CloudTrail alerts on delete calls. Versioning makes deletes reversible; MFA Delete makes them require the second factor.
Move the data off S3.
scenarios.why: The correct approach layers defenses: versioning turns deletes into reversible version markers, MFA Delete requires the physical second factor for permanent deletion, least-privilege limits who can delete, and alerting catches it fast. Moving off S3 abandons the platform's protections; laptop backups are not a strategy.
scenarios.hint: What would have made the delete reversible — or impossible without MFA?
evidence: 12,000 objects deleted; no versions; bucket had no MFA Delete

scenarios.title: The Shared Uploads
scenarios.situation: Three EC2 instances behind a load balancer let users upload images. Uploads land on local disk — users see different files depending on which instance serves them.
choices: Bigger disks on each instance.
Sync the disks with rsync every minute.
Use sticky sessions so users always hit the same instance.
Move uploads to EFS (shared NFS across instances/AZs) or S3: one shared namespace all instances see. EFS for filesystem semantics, S3 for object semantics — either ends the split-brain.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes local state from the scaling tier: shared storage (EFS or S3) gives every instance the same view. rsync races and diverges; sticky sessions break the load balancer's job and fail on instance replacement; bigger disks multiply the divergence.
scenarios.hint: What breaks when an instance is replaced by Auto Scaling?
evidence: User uploads image, refreshes, image gone (different instance served)

scenarios.title: The Private Share
scenarios.situation: Users need to download their private invoices (PDFs in a private bucket). The team proposes making the bucket public 'just for invoices.'
choices: Presigned URLs: the app (with bucket access) generates a time-limited URL per invoice per user. Bucket stays private; the URL expires. Verify the requesting user owns the invoice before signing.
Copy invoices to each user's laptop.
Public bucket with unguessable object names.
Email the PDFs as attachments.
scenarios.why: The correct approach keeps the bucket private and delegates temporary access: presigned URLs are cryptographically scoped to one object and expire. Unguessable names are security through obscurity; email attachments leak and bloat; laptop copies are unmanageable.
scenarios.hint: How do you grant temporary access without changing bucket permissions?
evidence: Private invoices; per-user access; links must expire

scenarios.title: The 60TB Move
scenarios.situation: A 60TB file server must migrate to S3. The office uplink is 100 Mbps and the deadline is 3 weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right transfer method?
choices: Upload over the office uplink and hope.

Order a Snowball Edge: ship the device, copy 60TB locally at LAN speed, ship it back — AWS loads it to S3. At 100 Mbps, 60TB takes ~55 days of continuous transfer; the deadline makes offline the only option.
DataSync over the uplink with compression.
Mail USB drives.
scenarios.why: The correct approach does the arithmetic: 60TB at 100 Mbps is roughly 55 days — the 3-week deadline kills online transfer regardless of tooling. Snowball Edge moves the bottleneck to LAN speed plus shipping. Compression helps but cannot beat physics; USB drives by mail have no chain of custody or tracking.
scenarios.hint: How long does 60TB take at 100 Mbps?

scenarios.title: The Tape Library
scenarios.situation: The company backs up to a physical tape library with VTL software. They want the same workflow but with cloud durability and no new backup software.
choices: Keep the physical tapes.
Rewrite the backup jobs for S3 APIs.
Tape Gateway: presents a virtual tape library to the existing backup software; tapes land in S3 and archive to Glacier. Same workflow, cloud backend — the hybrid bridge for tape estates.
DataSync the tape files.
scenarios.why: The correct approach preserves the workflow: Tape Gateway speaks VTL to the existing software, so no retraining and no rewrite, while tapes get S3 durability and Glacier economics. Rewriting backup jobs is months of risk; DataSync moves files, not tape workflows; keeping tapes keeps the problem.
scenarios.hint: What changes for the backup operator on Monday morning?
evidence: VTL backup software; 400 tapes; operators trained on tape workflow

domains.description: S3 classes and security, EBS/EFS/instance store, hybrid storage with Gateway and DataSync.

domains.name: Database Services

scenarios.title: The 3 AM Failover
scenarios.situation: The primary RDS instance's AZ has an outage. The app is down. The database is Single-AZ with no replicas.
scenarios.prompt: What should have been in place, and what now?
choices: Add a read replica now — it will take over.
Wait for the AZ to recover.
Restore from the latest snapshot to a new AZ — hours of downtime, data loss since the snapshot.

Multi-AZ: a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover (typically 1-2 minutes). Now: fail over manually if possible, restore to Multi-AZ after, and never run production Single-AZ again.
scenarios.why: The correct approach names the missing feature: Multi-AZ exists precisely for AZ failure with automatic failover. A read replica is async and needs promotion (and does not exist here); snapshot restore loses data and time; waiting surrenders the SLA. The lesson is architectural — HA is configured before the outage.
scenarios.hint: Which feature fails over automatically to a standby?
evidence: us-east-1a impaired; Single-AZ RDS down; RTO target 5 min

scenarios.title: The Read Storm
scenarios.situation: The product catalog DB (RDS) is at 95% CPU every afternoon — all reads. Writes are light. The app slows for everyone.
choices: Add RDS read replicas and point catalog reads at the reader endpoint; add ElastiCache in front for the hottest queries. Reads scale horizontally; the writer stays untouched.
Multi-AZ — the standby will help.
Throttle the users.
Bigger instance — vertically scale.
scenarios.why: The correct approach scales reads where reads happen: replicas absorb the read load, ElastiCache absorbs the hottest keys, and the primary breathes. Vertical scaling is expensive and finite; Multi-AZ's standby serves no reads; throttling users is surrender.
scenarios.hint: Is the bottleneck reads or writes?
evidence: CPU 95% 2-6pm; 98% queries are SELECTs on catalog tables

scenarios.title: The Spiky Sessions
scenarios.situation: Session storage: traffic is wildly unpredictable (10 to 10,000 rps), needs single-digit ms latency, and the team manages no servers.
choices: RDS with a big instance.
DynamoDB on-demand: serverless, scales to any request rate automatically, single-digit ms, pay per request — built for exactly this shape. Add DAX if hot keys need microseconds.
ElastiCache as the store.
A bigger EC2 with local files.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches serverless to spiky: on-demand DynamoDB absorbs 10-to-10000 rps swings with no capacity planning and no throttling. RDS needs provisioning for the peak (paying for idle); ElastiCache is a cache, not a store; local files do not scale or persist.
scenarios.hint: What happens at 3 AM when traffic is 10 rps — what do you pay?
evidence: 10 rps night, 10k rps peaks; sessions; ms latency required

scenarios.title: The Slow Catalog
scenarios.situation: The same 50 product queries run thousands of times per hour against RDS. The database is fine, but the queries add 200ms to every page.
choices: Rewrite the queries.
Add more read replicas.
ElastiCache (Redis) with cache-aside: check the cache, on miss query the DB and populate with a TTL. The 50 hot queries stop hitting the database entirely.
Bigger RDS instance.
scenarios.why: The correct approach caches the hot set: 50 repeated queries are the textbook cache-aside case — TTL-bounded, tiny memory, massive latency win. Bigger instances and more replicas scale the wrong layer; rewriting queries that are already fine misses the point.
scenarios.hint: How many distinct queries are actually slow?

scenarios.title: The Analytics Ask
scenarios.situation: Finance runs complex SQL over 5 years of transactions (2TB) every Monday. It currently runs on the production RDS and slows checkout.
choices: Run the queries at night.
Export to spreadsheets.
Bigger production RDS.
Redshift (or Redshift Serverless): move analytics off the transactional database into a columnar warehouse built for heavy SQL. ETL the data weekly; Monday queries stop touching checkout.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates OLAP from OLTP: Redshift's columnar MPP engine is built for 2TB analytics scans, and isolating the workload protects checkout latency. Bigger RDS mixes the workloads expensively; night scheduling still risks overlap; spreadsheets do not scale to 2TB.
scenarios.hint: Is this a transactions problem or an analytics problem?
evidence: 2TB, complex joins, weekly; production RDS CPU spikes during runs

scenarios.title: The Oracle Exit
scenarios.situation: The company must migrate Oracle (with stored procedures) to Aurora PostgreSQL with under 30 minutes of downtime.
choices: SCT to convert the schema and procedures, DMS full-load-plus-CDC to replicate with minimal lag, validate row counts and checksums, cut over in the window when lag is near zero.
Rewrite the app for DynamoDB instead.
Stay on Oracle.
Weekend big-bang: dump, convert by hand, load, hope.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses both tools for their jobs: SCT converts what DMS cannot (procedures, schema dialect), DMS CDC keeps the target current until cutover, validation proves fidelity before traffic moves. Big-bang risks the whole weekend; rewriting the app is a different project; staying avoids the question.
scenarios.hint: What converts the stored procedures — DMS or SCT?

scenarios.title: Aurora or RDS?
scenarios.situation: A new global SaaS app needs PostgreSQL compatibility, fast failover, read scaling to 10 replicas, and a future EU region.
choices: RDS PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ and read replicas.

Aurora PostgreSQL: storage auto-scales and replicates 6 ways across 3 AZs, failover is near-instant, up to 15 low-lag readers, and Global Database covers the EU future. RDS works, but Aurora is built for this shape.
DynamoDB — go NoSQL.
Self-managed PostgreSQL on EC2.
scenarios.why: The correct approach picks the cloud-native engine for cloud-native requirements: Aurora's storage-layer replication gives the failover and reader story RDS cannot match, and Global Database is the EU answer. RDS is fine for simpler needs; DynamoDB abandons the relational requirement; self-managed abandons the managed requirement.
scenarios.hint: Which requirements are about the storage layer vs the compute layer?
objectives: Plan for global from day one
evidence: PG-compatible; <30s failover; 10 read replicas; EU region later

domains.description: RDS Multi-AZ and replicas, Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, Redshift, DMS migrations.

domains.name: Networking

scenarios.title: The Flat Network
scenarios.situation: A startup runs web, app, and database all in one public subnet. The database has a public IP 'for debugging.'
choices: Add a second public subnet.
It works — leave it; add a stronger DB password.

3-tier VPC: ALB in public subnets, app servers in private subnets (NAT for outbound), RDS in isolated private subnets with no internet route. Security groups: DB only accepts from the app tier's group. Debugging via Session Manager, not public IPs.
Move the database to S3.
scenarios.why: The correct approach tiers by exposure: each layer only reachable from the one above, the database with no internet path at all. A strong password on a public database is one credential from breach; S3 is not a database; a second public subnet doubles the flatness.
scenarios.hint: Which tier should have no route to the internet?
evidence: Web+app+db in 10.0.1.0/24 public; db has Elastic IP

scenarios.title: The Blocked Deploy
scenarios.situation: App servers cannot reach the database after a security group change. The DB's SG allows 5432 from the app tier's CIDR block.
choices: PostgreSQL is down.
The VPC is misconfigured.
Open 5432 to 0.0.0.0/0 to test.

The CIDR-based rule broke when Auto Scaling replaced instances with new IPs outside the expected range. Fix: reference the app tier's security group as the source instead of CIDRs — group membership follows the instances.
scenarios.why: The correct approach suspects the brittle rule: CIDR-based inter-tier rules break as instances churn; source-group referencing is immune to IP changes. Database-down needs evidence; VPC blame is vague; opening to the world 'to test' is how breaches start.
scenarios.hint: What changed — the database, or the set of IPs?
evidence: SG updated yesterday; ASG replaced 4 instances overnight

scenarios.title: The Data Center Link
scenarios.situation: A company needs its on-prem data center connected to AWS: steady 4 Gbps, sensitive data, latency-sensitive. Setup time available: 2 months.
choices: Direct Connect: dedicated private fiber, consistent throughput, lower transfer pricing, no internet traversal — the steady/high-throughput/compliance answer. Two months is enough to provision it; use a VPN as interim if needed.
The public internet with TLS.
Snowball.
Site-to-Site VPN — quick and encrypted.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches steady-plus-sensitive to the dedicated link: Direct Connect gives consistent bandwidth and private path that VPN-over-internet cannot guarantee. VPN is the fast interim, not the steady-state answer; public internet fails the sensitivity bar; Snowball moves data, not networks.
scenarios.hint: Is the requirement steady throughput or quick setup?

scenarios.title: The Global Launch
scenarios.situation: Users in the US, EU, and Asia complain the app is slow. It runs in us-east-1 only, serving images from EC2.
choices: Bigger EC2 instances in us-east-1.
CloudFront in front of S3 for the images (edge caching worldwide) plus consider multi-region for the dynamic tier later. Static content via CDN is the first, highest-leverage global move.
More regions immediately for everything.
Tell users to use a VPN.
scenarios.why: The correct approach attacks the dominant latency: images from one region to Asia is physics, and CloudFront fixes it with edge caching. Bigger instances do not shorten distance; full multi-region on day one is over-engineering; VPNs add latency.
scenarios.hint: What is actually slow — the images, or the API?
evidence: Image-heavy pages 8s in Asia, 1.2s in US; API p95 300ms everywhere

scenarios.title: The Private Pipeline
scenarios.situation: EC2 instances in private subnets (no NAT) need to read deployment artifacts from S3. Currently failing.
choices: Add a NAT gateway.
Open the subnets to the internet.
Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint: private, free, no NAT needed — traffic to S3 stays on the AWS network. Update the route table for the endpoint.
Copy artifacts via the ALB.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses the purpose-built path: gateway endpoints give private S3 access with no internet, no NAT cost, and no bandwidth charges. NAT works but bills for the privilege; opening subnets defeats the isolation; the ALB is not a file pipe.
scenarios.hint: Does S3 traffic need the internet?
evidence: Private subnets, no NAT; S3 reads time out

scenarios.title: The Fifteen VPCs
scenarios.situation: The org has 15 VPCs (per-team) plus on-prem, all needing to talk. Currently 40 peering connections and growing.
choices: One giant VPC for everyone.
The internet between VPCs.
Keep peering — it works.
Transit Gateway: one hub, each VPC and the VPN/DX attach once; transitive routing in one place. 40+ peerings become 16 attachments with central route control.
scenarios.why: The correct approach replaces the peering mesh with a hub: attachments scale linearly, routes are centrally managed, and on-prem connects once. The mesh grows quadratically and has no transitive routing; one giant VPC destroys team isolation; internet routing fails every security review.
scenarios.hint: How many peerings does VPC #16 need in each design?
evidence: 15 VPCs, 40 peerings, on-prem VPN; 3 more teams onboarding

scenarios.title: The Region Failure
scenarios.situation: The app runs active-passive in two regions. During a regional outage, failover meant manually editing DNS — 40 minutes of downtime.
choices: Route 53 failover routing with health checks: DNS automatically shifts to the secondary when the primary's health check fails. No humans, no 40 minutes.
A bigger primary region.
Anycast IPs.
Faster manual edits — practice the runbook.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes the human from the failover path: health-checked DNS failover reacts in minutes, tested continuously. Faster manual edits still need a human awake; bigger regions still fail; anycast without health checks routes to the dead region.
scenarios.hint: Who should detect the failure — a human, or a health check?
evidence: Region outage; manual DNS change took 40 min; SLA 5 min

domains.description: VPC design, security groups vs NACLs, hybrid connectivity, Route 53, CloudFront.

domains.name: Monitoring and Observability

scenarios.title: Who Opened the Port?
scenarios.situation: A security group now allows SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. Nobody admits the change. The auditor wants the who and when.
choices: CloudTrail: lookup-events for AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress — it records the IAM identity, timestamp, and source IP of every API call. That is the audit trail.
CloudWatch metrics for the instance.
Ask in Slack again, louder.
VPC Flow Logs — they show the traffic.
scenarios.why: The correct approach queries the API audit trail: CloudTrail logs who-called-what with identity and time — exactly the auditor's question. Flow Logs show network traffic, not who changed the rule; metrics show performance; Slack is not an audit system.
scenarios.hint: Which service records API calls with identity?
evidence: sg-0abc allows 22 from 0.0.0.0/0; change made in last 7 days

scenarios.title: The Unencrypted Volumes
scenarios.situation: Policy: all EBS volumes must be encrypted. An audit finds 12 unencrypted volumes across 3 accounts.
choices: A monthly manual audit.
AWS Config rule (ENCRYPTED_VOLUMES) across the organization: continuously evaluates every volume, flags non-compliant ones, and can auto-remediate. One rule, always on — not a monthly spreadsheet.
CloudTrail alerts.
Trust the teams.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes compliance continuous: the Config rule evaluates state constantly and flags drift the hour it happens, with optional auto-remediation. Monthly audits leave 30-day windows; CloudTrail records actions, not state; trust is not a control.
scenarios.hint: Is the question about an action, or about current state?

scenarios.title: The Silent Outage
scenarios.situation: The checkout API was down for 40 minutes. CloudWatch had the metrics — nobody was notified.
choices: More logs.
More metrics.

An alarm with an action: threshold on the golden signal (5xx rate / latency), evaluation periods to avoid noise, and an SNS action paging the on-call with a runbook link. Metrics without alarms are history books.
A bigger dashboard.
scenarios.why: The correct approach closes the loop: metrics existed, but nothing evaluated them or notified anyone. The alarm anatomy — signal, threshold, evaluation, action — turns data into response. Dashboards and logs help diagnosis after someone knows; the alarm is what tells them.
scenarios.hint: What turns a metric into a wake-up?
evidence: 5xx 100% for 40 min; metric existed; zero notifications

scenarios.title: The Cron Server
scenarios.situation: A nightly report runs from cron on an EC2 instance. The instance was terminated during a cleanup — three nights of reports missed.
choices: Cron on two instances for redundancy.
Manual reports.
A bigger EC2 instance for cron.
EventBridge scheduled rule triggering Lambda: serverless cron — no instance to terminate, no server to patch, retries built in. The schedule lives in AWS, not on a box.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes the server from the schedule: EventBridge cron plus Lambda has no instance to clean up, no patching, and built-in retry. Bigger instances still get terminated; two crons double the ops; manual is regression.
scenarios.hint: What owned the schedule — the job, or a server?
evidence: cron host terminated; 3 missed nightly reports

scenarios.title: The Slow Checkout
scenarios.situation: Checkout p99 is 4 seconds. The team argues: frontend blames the API, API blames the database, database looks fine.
choices: X-Ray distributed tracing: follow one checkout request across the hops — the trace shows exactly where the 4 seconds go. Attribution beats argument.
Bigger instances everywhere.
Rewrite the checkout.
Add more logging everywhere.
scenarios.why: The correct approach measures instead of debating: the trace attributes latency per hop, ending the blame cycle with data. More logging without correlation is noise; bigger instances treat the wrong layer; rewrites without diagnosis repeat the problem.
scenarios.hint: Which hop owns the 4 seconds?
evidence: p99 4s checkout; each team blames another; no traces

scenarios.title: Is It Us or AWS?
scenarios.situation: Multiple services error simultaneously across two AZs. The team starts rolling back the morning's deploy.
choices: The deploy diff.
Personal Health Dashboard and the Service Health Dashboard: if AWS reports an issue affecting your resources, the deploy did not cause it. Check before rolling back a good deploy.
Roll back first, ask later.
Restart everything.
scenarios.why: The correct approach checks the platform before blaming the change: simultaneous multi-service errors across AZs smell like a platform issue, and Personal Health confirms it in seconds. Rolling back a good deploy during an AWS event adds risk; restarts and diffs come after the platform is ruled out.
scenarios.hint: What fails across services and AZs at once?
evidence: EC2 + RDS errors 10:42; deploy was 09:00, healthy for 90 min

scenarios.title: The Needle in the Logs
scenarios.situation: An intermittent 500 error hits 0.1% of requests. The logs are 50GB/day across 20 instances.
choices: Wait for it to get worse.
Download the logs and grep locally.
CloudWatch Logs Insights: query the centralized logs — filter for 500s, aggregate by endpoint and 5-minute bins, find the pattern. Centralized plus queryable beats 20 boxes of grep.
Increase log verbosity.
scenarios.why: The correct approach queries instead of downloading: Logs Insights scans 50GB in seconds and the aggregation reveals the pattern (one endpoint, one AZ, one deploy version). Local grep does not scale; more verbosity adds noise; waiting is not a strategy.
scenarios.hint: Where are the logs, and how do you ask questions of 50GB?

domains.description: CloudWatch metrics/alarms/logs, CloudTrail vs Config, EventBridge, X-Ray, health dashboards.

domains.name: Billing and Cost Management

scenarios.title: The Surprise Bill
scenarios.situation: The monthly bill jumps from $3,000 to $11,000. Nobody knows why. Finance wants answers by Friday.
choices: Blame the developers.
Delete random resources until it drops.
Pay it and hope next month is normal.

Cost Explorer: group by service, then by day — find the service and the start date of the spike. Drill by tag/region. Fix the cause (often a forgotten resource or a misconfigured service), then set Budgets and Anomaly Detection so it never surprises again.
scenarios.why: The correct approach investigates before acting: Cost Explorer's service-by-day view isolates the spike's source and start time in minutes. Random deletion risks production; blame is not analysis; hoping is not a strategy. The follow-through (Budgets + Anomaly Detection) converts the incident into prevention.
scenarios.hint: What changed, when, and in which service?

scenarios.title: The Chargeback Fight
scenarios.situation: Three teams share one AWS account. Finance needs each team's spend for chargeback, but 60% of resources are untagged.
choices: Enforce tag policies (Team, Project) via Organizations, activate the tags in billing, backfill what you can, and use Cost Explorer/CUR sliced by tag. Even splits punish efficient teams and reward waste.
One account per team retroactively.
Estimate from memory.
Split the bill evenly — close enough.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes spend attributable: enforced tags at creation plus activated allocation tags turn the bill into per-team numbers. Even splits destroy accountability incentives; retroactive account splits do not fix history; memory is not accounting.
scenarios.hint: Who should pay for the idle GPU instance nobody claims?

scenarios.title: The Expensive Experiment
scenarios.situation: A developer launched 20 p4d GPU instances in dev 'to test something' — $600/hour until someone noticed Monday.
choices: Trust developers more carefully.
SCP on the Dev OU denying expensive instance families (p*, x*, large GPU types) plus a Budget with an action at 120% forecasted. Guardrail blocks the launch; budget catches what guardrails miss.
Remove all dev access.
Weekly manual instance audits.
scenarios.why: The correct approach layers prevention and detection: the SCP makes the launch impossible (deny beats any Allow), the budget alerts before the weekend becomes a $30k lesson. Trust is not a control; removing access kills productivity; weekly audits find Monday's bill on Friday.
scenarios.hint: Should the control block the launch, or notice it Monday?

scenarios.title: The Steady Baseline
scenarios.situation: The fleet runs 100 m5.xlarge 24/7/365 — all On-Demand. The CFO asks why the bill never drops.
choices: Smaller instances.
Move it all to Spot.

3-year Compute Savings Plan covering the steady baseline: up to 72% off On-Demand for committed $/hour, flexible across families and regions. Keep On-Demand for the variable fringe above the baseline.
Turn everything off at night.
scenarios.why: The correct approach commits to what is certain: 100 instances 24/7 is the definition of committable baseline, and Savings Plans price it at up to 72% off while staying flexible. Spot cannot host the steady production baseline; night shutdowns do not apply to 24/7; smaller instances need rightsizing data first.
scenarios.hint: What portion of the fleet is truly 24/7?

scenarios.title: The 2 AM Outage
scenarios.situation: Production is down at 2 AM with a suspected AWS-side issue. The account has Basic support. The team debates opening a forum post.
scenarios.prompt: What should the support posture have been?
choices: Enterprise for everyone.
Page the CTO instead.
Basic is fine — forums are fast.

Business support minimum for production: 24/7 phone/chat, <1h response for urgent, plus Infrastructure Event Management for planned events. The 2 AM outage is exactly what the tier exists for — and it should have been in place before the outage.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches tier to criticality: production workloads need 24/7 human support with urgent SLAs — Basic has no one to call at 2 AM. Enterprise for everything overspends; the CTO cannot fix AWS-side issues; forums are not incident response.
scenarios.hint: Who do you call at 2 AM on Basic?
evidence: Prod down 02:00; suspected AWS-side; Basic support; no TAM

scenarios.title: The Idle Giants
scenarios.situation: Trusted Advisor flags 30 EC2 instances averaging 4% CPU and 40 unattached EBS volumes. The team says 'we might need them.'
choices: Right-size per Compute Optimizer (downsize the 4% instances), snapshot-and-delete the unattached volumes, and set a policy: idle 30 days gets flagged, 60 gets reclaimed. 'Might need' is not a capacity plan.
Delete everything immediately.
Bigger instances for headroom.
Keep everything — storage is cheap and CPU might spike.
scenarios.why: The correct approach acts on the data with a safety net: rightsizing follows the optimizer's numbers, snapshots make volume deletion reversible, and the policy prevents regrowth. Keeping everything is paying for nothing; immediate deletion without snapshots is reckless; bigger instances worsen the waste.
scenarios.hint: What is the cost of 'might need them' per month?
evidence: 30 instances @4% CPU; 40 unattached volumes; 2TB old snapshots

scenarios.title: The Data Center Refresh
scenarios.situation: The data center needs a $2M hardware refresh. Leadership asks: rebuy or move to AWS?
choices: On-prem is always cheaper at scale — rebuy.

3-year TCO with the Pricing Calculator: model the real workload (compute, storage, transfer, support), add the on-prem side fully loaded (hardware, power, cooling, space, staff, refresh cycle), and compare honestly — including migration cost and the agility value. No slogans, a spreadsheet.
Ask a vendor.
AWS is always cheaper — move.
scenarios.why: The correct approach prices both sides completely: most 'cloud is expensive' analyses omit on-prem staff/power/refresh, and most 'cloud is cheap' pitches omit transfer and the migration itself. The calculator plus a fully loaded on-prem model — reviewed by finance — is the only honest answer. Slogans are not analysis.
scenarios.hint: What is missing from each side's math?
evidence: $2M refresh vs cloud; 200 VMs; 5-yr horizon; regulated industry

domains.description: Pricing models, Cost Explorer and Budgets, Organizations, cost allocation, support plans.

domains.name: Architecture Best Practices

scenarios.title: Name the Pillar
scenarios.situation: The team proposes cutting the second AZ 'to save money' on the checkout database. The architect objects.
scenarios.prompt: Which pillar is the architect defending, and what is the trade?
choices: Operational Excellence — fewer AZs to operate.
Cost Optimization — the cut is correct.

Reliability: the second AZ is automatic failover for the checkout database. The trade is explicit — save money vs survive an AZ failure — and for checkout, Reliability outranks the savings. Name the trade, price both sides, decide deliberately.
Sustainability — fewer AZs, less energy.
scenarios.why: The correct approach frames it as a pillar trade-off, not a veto: Reliability (survive AZ failure) vs Cost Optimization (save the standby cost). For checkout — revenue — the reliability side usually wins, but the value is in making the trade explicit and priced rather than cutting blindly.
scenarios.hint: What breaks if the AZ fails, and what does the standby cost?
evidence: Cut RDS Multi-AZ; saves $400/mo; checkout DB

scenarios.title: The Thundering Herd
scenarios.situation: A flash sale hammers the order API: it calls inventory, payment, and email synchronously. Everything slows, then timeouts cascade.
choices: More database connections.
Rate-limit the customers harder.
Bigger API instances.

SQS between the API and the workers: the API validates and enqueues, workers process at their pace. Spikes queue up instead of cascading; each downstream scales independently. Add DLQs for poison messages.
scenarios.why: The correct approach breaks the synchronous chain: the queue absorbs the spike (that is what queues are for), workers scale on queue depth, and a slow email service no longer blocks payments. Bigger instances move the bottleneck; more connections treat the symptom; harsh rate limits turn away the sale.
scenarios.hint: What happens to an order when the email service is slow?
evidence: Flash sale 20x; sync chain; cascading timeouts; lost orders

scenarios.title: The Three Notifications
scenarios.situation: Every order must trigger: a confirmation email, an SMS, and an analytics event. Currently three sequential API calls in the order code.
choices: SNS fan-out: publish one order event to a topic; email, SMS, and analytics subscribe independently (via SQS queues or Lambda). Adding a fourth notification touches nothing existing; one slow subscriber never blocks the others.
Threads in the order service.
A bigger order service.
Keep the calls — they work.
scenarios.why: The correct approach publishes once and fans out: each subscriber evolves independently, failures isolate, and new notifications subscribe without code changes. Sequential calls couple every notification's latency and fate to the order path; threads complicate the service; bigger instances do not decouple.
scenarios.hint: What breaks when the SMS provider is slow?
evidence: order() calls email(); sms(); analytics(); — 900ms added, SMS outage blocks orders

scenarios.title: The RTO Argument
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants 'zero downtime ever' (active/active, $40k/mo). The app's actual requirement: back online within 4 hours, lose at most 1 hour of data.
choices: Active/active — leadership asked for it.

Backup-and-restore or pilot light: RTO 4h/RPO 1h is met by the cheapest rungs — automated backups plus tested restore, or replicated DB with AMIs ready. Active/active at 10x the cost buys recovery you do not need. Show the ladder, pick the rung, test it.
No DR — 4 hours is plenty to figure it out live.
Warm standby just in case.
scenarios.why: The correct approach prices the requirement: RTO/RPO numbers select the rung, and 4h/1h sits at the cheap end. Active/active for a 4-hour RTO is gold-plating; no DR gambles the business; warm standby overshoots without justification. The ladder plus a tested restore is the defensible answer.
scenarios.hint: What do the numbers actually require?
evidence: RTO 4h, RPO 1h; current: no DR plan; leadership wants active/active

scenarios.title: The Snowflake Prod
scenarios.situation: Production was built by console clicks over 2 years. Nobody can reproduce it, and the staging environment 'is kind of similar.'
choices: Hire someone who remembers the clicks.
Document the console clicks in a wiki.

Adopt IaC incrementally: template new resources in CloudFormation first, then import existing ones (drift detection shows the gaps), converge staging and prod on the same templates. Reproducibility comes from code, not documentation of clicks.
Rebuild prod from scratch over a weekend.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes the infrastructure reproducible without the big-bang rewrite: new resources templated from today, existing ones imported and drift-checked into alignment. Wiki documentation rots; weekend rebuilds are high-risk theater; human memory is not infrastructure.
scenarios.hint: How do you prove staging matches prod?
evidence: 2 years of console-built prod; staging 'kind of similar'; 3 outages from config drift

scenarios.title: The Sticky Sessions
scenarios.situation: The app stores shopping carts in server memory with sticky sessions. Auto Scaling replacements lose carts; users complain.
choices: Bigger instances so replacements are rarer.
Disable Auto Scaling.
Longer stickiness duration.

Externalize state: carts in DynamoDB or ElastiCache, sessions via tokens — compute becomes stateless, any instance serves any user, replacements lose nothing. Sticky sessions fight the platform's elasticity.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes state from the scaling tier: external session state makes every instance interchangeable — the foundation Auto Scaling assumes. Longer stickiness prolongs the mismatch; bigger instances delay it; disabling scaling surrenders elasticity.
scenarios.hint: What does an instance replacement destroy?
evidence: Carts vanish after deploys/scaling events; sticky sessions enabled

scenarios.title: The Blind Update
scenarios.situation: A CloudFormation stack update will run tonight. Nobody knows exactly what it will change — 'probably just the instance type.'
scenarios.prompt: What do you do before applying?
choices: Create a change set first: it previews every addition, modification, and replacement. Instance type changes can trigger replacement (new instance, data loss if unhandled) — the preview shows it before it happens.
Apply to prod first, it is faster.
Skip the update.
Apply it — CloudFormation is safe.
scenarios.why: The correct approach previews before applying: change sets list replacements explicitly, and replacement semantics (new resource, old deleted) are where updates bite. Blind applies gamble on 'probably'; prod-first inverts the safety order; skipping avoids the question.
scenarios.hint: Which resources will be replaced vs updated in place?
evidence: Update tonight; change: instance type + SG rule; no change set created

domains.name: Migration Planning

scenarios.title: The Big-Bang Proposal
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants all 200 servers migrated in one weekend to 'get it over with.'
choices: Pilot plus waves: migrate one low-risk app first to prove the runbook, then factory-model waves by dependency and risk. 200 servers in one weekend has one outcome — a very long weekend. Waves de-risk and build velocity.
Migrate half per weekend.
Delay a year.
Agree — speed matters.
scenarios.why: The correct approach industrializes the migration: the pilot validates tooling and runbooks on low stakes, waves order by dependency (ADS data) so shared databases do not strand apps, and each wave is small enough to roll back. Halving the big bang halves nothing about the risk profile.
scenarios.hint: What is the blast radius of wave one vs the big bang?
evidence: 200 servers, unknown dependencies, one weekend proposed

scenarios.title: The Oracle Exit Plan
scenarios.situation: Oracle licensing costs are exploding. The 800GB database with 200 stored procedures must move to Aurora PostgreSQL.
choices: DMS alone — it migrates databases.

SCT plus DMS: SCT converts the schema and stored procedures (and flags what needs manual work), DMS replicates the data with CDC for minimal-downtime cutover. DMS moves data; SCT converts dialect — heterogeneous needs both.
Manual rewrite over a year.
Stay on Oracle.
scenarios.why: The correct approach assigns each tool its job: 200 stored procedures do not convert themselves, and SCT's assessment tells you the manual work upfront. DMS alone leaves you with data and no working procedures; manual rewrite is a different project measured in years.
scenarios.hint: What converts the 200 stored procedures?
evidence: Oracle 19c, 800GB, 200 procedures; licensing renewal in 6 months

scenarios.title: The Math Problem
scenarios.situation: 80TB must move in 4 weeks over a 200 Mbps uplink. The team started a DataSync task 'and hopes.'
choices: Upgrade the uplink permanently.
Hope is fine — DataSync is fast.

80TB at 200 Mbps is roughly 37 days of continuous transfer — past the deadline before contention and overhead. Stop, order Snowball Edge devices, copy at LAN speed, ship back. Do the math before the tooling.
Compress harder.
scenarios.why: The correct approach computes first: the transfer time exceeds the deadline, so no online tooling fixes it — physics wins. Snowball moves the bottleneck to LAN plus shipping. Compression helps at the margins; permanent uplink upgrades take longer than the deadline.
scenarios.hint: How many days is 80TB at 200 Mbps?

scenarios.title: The Status Meeting
scenarios.situation: The migration has 5 tools running (DMS, DataSync, manual scripts). Leadership asks for a status — nobody can answer.
choices: More status meetings.
One tool for everything.
A bigger spreadsheet.
Migration Hub: register every migration with it — DMS tasks, DataSync, server migrations all report status centrally. One console answers leadership; the spreadsheet was stale at creation.
scenarios.why: The correct approach gives leadership one live view: Migration Hub aggregates progress across tools instead of five separate consoles and a spreadsheet. More meetings multiply the confusion; one tool cannot do discovery, database replication, and file sync.
scenarios.hint: Where is the single pane of glass?
evidence: 5 tools, 40 servers in flight, leadership blind

scenarios.title: The Partner Feed
scenarios.situation: A partner has sent nightly CSVs via SFTP for 10 years and will not change. The files must land in S3 and trigger processing.
choices: Transfer Family: managed SFTP with the files landing directly in S3 — no servers to patch, no cron to babysit. S3 event triggers the processing Lambda. The partner changes nothing.
Ask the partner to use the S3 console.
Email the CSVs.
An EC2 instance running OpenSSH with a cron copy.
scenarios.why: The correct approach keeps the partner's workflow intact while removing your servers: Transfer Family speaks SFTP and writes to S3 natively, and S3 events drive processing. Self-managed SSH is undifferentiated ops; the console is not an integration; email is not a pipeline.
scenarios.hint: What changes for the partner on Monday?
evidence: Nightly CSV via SFTP, 10-year history, partner will not change

scenarios.title: The Failed Cutover
scenarios.situation: Wave 2 cutover: error rate hits 5% and climbing. The team debates whether to 'wait and see.'
scenarios.prompt: What should have been decided already?
choices: Whether 5% is really that bad.

The rollback trigger — defined before the wave (e.g., error rate above 2% for 15 minutes triggers DNS flip-back to the old environment). 5% and climbing meets it: execute the rollback, then diagnose. Debate is what the trigger replaces.
Who to blame.
A longer maintenance window.
scenarios.why: The correct approach executes the pre-decided trigger: rollback criteria exist precisely so 2 AM decisions are mechanical, not debates. 5% climbing is unambiguous. Blame and window extensions do not restore service; the trigger does.
scenarios.hint: What was the abort criteria for this wave?
evidence: Error rate 5% climbing; no pre-defined abort criteria

scenarios.title: The Greenfield Org
scenarios.situation: A new company starts on AWS: 4 teams, regulated data, no existing accounts.
choices: VPC first, accounts later.
One account, IAM users, go.

Control Tower landing zone: management account plus Security OU (audit, log-archive), team OUs with guardrails, Account Factory for new accounts. Regulated data demands the audit trail and isolation from day one — retrofitting it later is the expensive path.
Four separate payers.
scenarios.why: The correct approach builds governance before workloads: the landing zone bakes in the audit trail, log immutability, and account isolation that regulators will ask about. One account mixes everything irreversibly; separate payers lose consolidated billing; VPCs are per-account resources — accounts come first.
scenarios.hint: What will the auditor ask about in 18 months?
evidence: 4 teams, regulated data, zero accounts today

scenarios.title: Whose Patch Is It?
scenarios.situation: A vulnerability is found in the PostgreSQL engine version running on RDS. Who patches it?
scenarios.prompt: According to the shared responsibility model, who is responsible?
choices: Nobody — RDS auto-patches silently with no action.
The OS vendor.
The customer — it is their database.

AWS — engine patching on RDS is AWS's responsibility (security OF the managed service). The customer owns credentials, security groups, parameter groups, and backup configuration — security IN the cloud.
scenarios.why: The correct approach places the split line: on RDS, AWS owns the engine and host patching; the customer owns access, network, and configuration. 'The customer' confuses RDS with EC2 (where the guest OS is yours); silent auto-patching still involves maintenance windows you schedule.
scenarios.hint: Is RDS IaaS or a managed service — and what does that move?
evidence: PostgreSQL engine vulnerability; workload on RDS Multi-AZ

scenarios.title: The Qualifier Trap
scenarios.situation: Question: 'A company needs shared file storage for 50 EC2 instances with least operational overhead. Which is MOST appropriate?' Options include S3, EBS, EFS, and instance store.
scenarios.prompt: What is the answer and why?
choices: EFS — 'shared file storage' plus 'least operational overhead' maps exactly: managed NFS, no servers, scales automatically. S3 is object storage (no filesystem), EBS attaches to one instance, instance store is ephemeral.
Instance store — fastest.
S3 — it is the cheapest.
EBS — attach to all instances.
scenarios.why: The correct approach lets the qualifier choose: 'shared file storage' eliminates S3 (objects) and EBS (single-attach) and instance store (ephemeral); 'least operational overhead' confirms the managed service. S3 is the classic distractor — right vendor, wrong storage class.
scenarios.hint: Which two words in the question eliminate three options?
evidence: 'shared file storage for 50 EC2 instances with least operational overhead'

scenarios.title: Most Cost-Effective?
scenarios.situation: Question: 'Archive 50TB of compliance data, accessed maybe once a year, MOST cost-effective.'
choices: S3 Standard — simple.

S3 Glacier Deep Archive — ~$1/TB-month, retrieval in hours, which fits 'maybe once a year' compliance restores. The qualifier 'most cost-effective' plus 'rarely accessed' selects the cheapest tier that meets the need.
EBS snapshots.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches tier to access: Deep Archive is purpose-built for compliance archives with hourly retrieval tolerance. Standard is 20x the price for unread data; snapshots are for volumes, not archives; Intelligent-Tiering adds monitoring fees for data with a known-frozen pattern.
scenarios.hint: What does 'maybe once a year' tell you about retrieval urgency?

scenarios.title: The Urgent Ticket
scenarios.situation: Question: 'A production workload needs 24/7 support with 1-hour response for urgent issues. MOST cost-effective plan?'
choices: Basic — it is free.
Developer — cheapest paid.
Business — 24/7 phone/chat with <1h urgent response; the minimum tier meeting the requirement, and therefore the most cost-effective one that qualifies.
Enterprise — best support.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies 'most cost-effective' as 'cheapest that meets the requirement': Basic has no humans, Developer is business-hours only, Enterprise overshoots. Business is the floor for production urgency — memorize it as the production-minimum tier.
scenarios.hint: Which is the cheapest tier that actually meets '24/7, 1-hour urgent'?

scenarios.title: The Clock Problem
scenarios.situation: You are 45 minutes in with 35 questions left. Several flagged hard ones remain.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right pacing move?
choices: Rush through all 35 in 10 minutes.
Leave the hard ones blank to avoid wrong answers.
Spend the remaining time on the flagged hard ones — they are worth more.

Keep the 3-pass rhythm: answer the remaining confident ones fast, make educated guesses on the rest — never leave blanks (no penalty). A guessed question and a skipped question score the same except the guess can be right.
scenarios.why: The correct approach protects expected value: every answered question can score, blanks cannot, and there is no guessing penalty. The 3-pass rhythm banks confident points first; perfectionism on hard questions starves easy ones. All questions are worth the same — act like it.
scenarios.hint: What is the expected value of a blank vs a guess?
evidence: 45 min left, 35 questions, several flagged hard

scenarios.title: The Overhead Question
scenarios.situation: Question: 'Run a relational database with LEAST operational overhead.' Options: EC2 with PostgreSQL, RDS PostgreSQL, Aurora Serverless v2, DynamoDB.
choices: Aurora Serverless v2 — managed engine plus automatic scaling with no capacity planning; the least operational overhead among the relational options. DynamoDB is less overhead but not relational — the distractor.
DynamoDB — least overhead overall.
EC2 with PostgreSQL — full control.
RDS PostgreSQL — managed, but still provisioned.
scenarios.why: The correct approach honors both constraints: 'relational' eliminates DynamoDB (the trap — least overhead but wrong data model), and 'least operational overhead' picks Serverless v2 over provisioned RDS. EC2 is maximum control and maximum overhead.
scenarios.hint: Which option violates 'relational' — and which minimizes overhead among the rest?

scenarios.title: The Final 48 Hours
scenarios.situation: The exam is in 2 days. You are strong on compute and networking, shaky on billing and migration specifics.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best use of the time?
choices: Learn a new domain (databases) for breadth.

Targeted review: drill billing and migration (the weak spots) with scenarios, rewrite the brain-dump splits from memory until fluent, light review of strengths, sleep well. Depth on weak spots beats breadth on new ones.
Retake every domain equally.
Cram all night before.
scenarios.why: The correct approach invests where the marginal point lives: weak domains have the most recoverable points, the brain dump converts recall to fluency, and sleep protects exam-day retrieval. New domains risk shallow confusion; equal retakes waste time on strengths; cramming destroys recall.
scenarios.hint: Where is the next point cheapest to earn?

Start building immediately — planning wastes lab time.
Attempt the most impressive architecture possible to stand out.
