lessons.title: Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy — Core concepts
concepts: Disposition the portfolio with the 6 R's — rehost, replatform, repurchase, refactor, retain, retire — choosing the least-disruptive strategy that captures real value per application. Blanket strategies (all-rehost, all-rewrite) are how migrations fail.

Use the Cloud Adoption Framework to assign ownership: Business (value), People (skills), Governance (oversight), Platform (landing zone), Security (controls), Operations (runbooks). Migrations stall on the non-technical perspectives more often than the technical ones.

Build the landing zone before the first workload: Organizations with OUs, separate accounts per environment/workload, Identity Center SSO, centralized CloudTrail/Config logging, and SCP guardrails. Retrofitting foundations under live workloads is surgery.

Compare TCO honestly: all on-prem costs (hardware, power, cooling, space, staff, refresh, downtime) against all cloud costs (compute, storage, transfer, support, growth, migration) over the same horizon. Omitted line items are how both sides lie with numbers.

Migrate in dependency-ordered waves: discover with Application Discovery Service, pilot on simple apps, group dependents with their dependencies, and put core systems last with rollback criteria. Then optimize — refactor the seams where the business case is proven, strangler-fig style.

example.code:
aws organizations list-roots --query 'Roots[*].Id'
aws organizations list-organizational-units-for-parent --parent-id r-xxxx \
  --query 'OrganizationalUnits[*].Name'
example.walkthrough: Listing the organization root and OUs shows the account structure behind the landing zone — workloads isolated by account, guardrails attached at the OU level. If every workload lives in one flat account, the foundation was skipped.

pitfalls: Common trap: migrating before the landing zone exists — every workload then inherits missing SSO, logging, and guardrails.
Common trap: TCO comparisons that omit data transfer, staff time, or the migration itself — the side with more hidden costs always 'wins.'
Common trap: big-bang cutovers for dependency-heavy systems — one failed cutover rolls back everything at once.
Common trap: refactoring as a migration prerequisite — combine rewrite risk with migration risk and both slip; rehost, then strangler-fig.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Aws Cloud Practitioner Plus move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy
concepts: Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy is a multi-step process within Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy to the broader Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:

  Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing

example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it top to bottom: each domain builds on the previous one, and later scenarios assume earlier knowledge
Every lesson ends with a knowledge check: answer correctly and the lesson auto-completes. Wrong answers send you back to review — this is verification, not clicking through
Scenarios are timed decision exercises with evidence to examine. Treat each like the real thing: read everything, decide, then commit
Your progress saves automatically. Domains unlock as you complete prerequisites — the path guides you, but you set the pace

example.code:
LEARN path: lessons -> scenarios -> labs -> drills
TERMINAL: hands-on command practice
MOCK: full timed assessment when ready

Suggested daily loop:
  1. Complete 2-3 lessons (with knowledge checks)
  2. Work 3-5 scenarios in those domains

example.walkthrough: The bootcamp mirrors how professionals actually work: learn the concept, apply it under realistic conditions, then prove it in the lab. Skipping straight to the mock without the lessons is the fastest way to fail it.

Treating the knowledge check as a formality instead of a real self-test
Ignoring the terminal and labs — hands-on reps are where durable skill comes from

lessons.title: assessment Strategy: How to Win

Sleep and spacing beat cramming: 90-minute focused sessions with breaks outperform marathon sessions, especially the week before assessment day

example.code:
The 3-pass method for timed assessments:

  Pass 2 (40% of time): work the flagged mediums with evidence

Never spend 10 minutes on one question while five easy ones wait.

Perfectionism on one hard question while easy points expire
Studying new material the night before instead of reviewing what you know

lessons.title: IAM Identities: Users, Groups, and Roles
concepts: IAM users represent people or applications with long-term credentials — create one per human, never share
IAM groups collect users by job function: attach permissions to groups, not users — onboarding becomes add-to-group
IAM roles provide temporary credentials: assumed by users, applications, or AWS services — no long-term secrets to rotate or leak
EC2 instance profiles and Lambda execution roles: services assume roles for permissions — the standard for workload identity
The root user: lock it with MFA, never use it daily, never create access keys for it

example.walkthrough: The policy allows one action on one bucket prefix — attached to the ReportReaders group, not to individuals. New analysts get access by joining the group. The comment states the workload rule: EC2 and Lambda never hold access keys; they assume roles and get temporary credentials the platform rotates automatically.

pitfalls: Attaching policies directly to users — unmanageable past a handful of people; use groups
Long-term access keys on EC2 instances — use instance profiles and roles instead
Daily use of the root account — compromise of root is total compromise; MFA it and lock it away
lessons.try_it: List the IAM users in a sandbox account and identify any with policies attached directly instead of via groups.

lessons.title: IAM Policies: The JSON Anatomy
concepts: Policy structure: Version, Statement array of Effect (Allow/Deny), Action, Resource, optional Condition
Evaluation logic: default deny; an explicit Allow permits; an explicit Deny overrides everything — Deny always wins
Managed policies (AWS-managed, customer-managed) are reusable and versioned; inline policies embed in one identity — prefer managed
Resource scoping: arn:aws:s3:::bucket/* vs * — the narrower the resource, the smaller the blast radius
Policy Simulator: test what a policy actually allows before deploying — the fastest way to debug AccessDenied

example.walkthrough: Read the three statements as a story: broad read-only describe, start/stop limited to dev-tagged instances in one region, and an explicit Deny on termination that overrides any Allow elsewhere. The Condition key is the precision instrument — tag-based scoping without writing a policy per instance.

pitfalls: Action * with Resource * (AdministratorAccess) on a workload role — the blast radius of a compromise is the whole account
Forgetting explicit Deny wins — a Deny in any attached policy blocks, no matter how many Allows exist
Inline policies copied across users — drift and sprawl; use customer-managed policies
lessons.try_it: Write a policy allowing s3:GetObject on one bucket prefix only, then test it in the Policy Simulator.

lessons.title: Least Privilege in Practice
concepts: Least privilege: grant only the permissions needed, nothing more — the single highest-leverage security practice on AWS
Start with AWS-managed job-function policies, then narrow: they are broad by design
IAM Access Analyzer generates policies from actual CloudTrail activity — run the workload, generate the policy, deploy the narrowed version
Permission boundaries: cap what an identity can ever get, even if other policies allow more — the guardrail for delegated administration
Review on a cadence: unused permissions accumulate; Access Analyzer unused-access findings flag what to remove

example.code:
# Generate a least-privilege policy from real usage
aws accessanalyzer start-policy-generation \
  --policy-generation-details principalArn=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AppRole
# Review the generated JSON, then attach as a customer-managed policy.
# Permission boundary: cap a developer role so it can never touch IAM
# or production-tagged resources, regardless of other policies.
example.walkthrough: The workflow is generate-from-reality: let the role run its real workload, have Access Analyzer build the policy from the CloudTrail trail, review it, and attach the narrowed result. Permission boundaries are the second layer — they cap the maximum possible permissions, so even a mistaken Allow cannot escape the guardrail.

pitfalls: Starting from AdministratorAccess and narrowing later — later never comes; start narrow
Ignoring unused-access findings — every unused permission is breach blast radius
No permission boundaries on roles developers create — one bad policy from privilege escalation
lessons.try_it: Run Access Analyzer's unused access check on one role and remove one permission it flags.

lessons.title: IAM Identity Center and Federation
concepts: IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS SSO): one login for all accounts and applications — short-term credentials per account
Federation with SAML 2.0 or OIDC: your corporate IdP is the identity source — no IAM users for employees
Permission sets: define permissions once, assign to users and groups per account — consistent access across the organization
Why not IAM users for humans: long-term keys get leaked, shared, and forgotten — federation eliminates the key class entirely
ABAC with session tags: pass department and project as session tags, write one policy using aws:PrincipalTag — scales to thousands

example.code:
# Permission set: one definition, many accounts
# Identity Center > Permission sets > Create > e.g. 'DataAnalyst'
# Attach AWS-managed + custom policies once, assign to groups per account.
# Users: portal login -> click account -> CLI/console with short-term
# credentials (aws sso login). No access keys anywhere.
example.walkthrough: The model inverts the old way: instead of IAM users in every account, define a permission set once and assign it to IdP groups per account. Users sign in at the portal and get short-lived credentials. There are no access keys to leak because none exist — the entire leaked-key incident class disappears for human access.

pitfalls: Creating IAM users for every employee in every account — key sprawl and offboarding gaps; federate instead
Permission sets copied per account with drift — define once, assign many
No MFA at the IdP — federation is only as strong as the identity source; enforce phishing-resistant MFA there
lessons.try_it: Map your team's access: which IAM users could become a permission set assignment instead?

lessons.title: MFA, Conditions, and Access Analyzer
concepts: MFA enforcement via policy condition: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent=false -> Deny — stolen password without MFA means no access
Require MFA for the riskiest actions: iam:* changes, S3 deletes with MFA Delete on versioned buckets
Condition keys are the fine print: aws:SourceIp, aws:RequestedRegion, aws:PrincipalTag — scope permissions by context, not just identity
Access Analyzer for S3 and IAM: flags public buckets, cross-account access, and unused permissions — the continuous audit
MFA Delete on S3: versioned bucket deletes require MFA — ransomware and accidents both need the second factor

example.walkthrough: The Deny statement is the MFA gate: any request without MFA is denied regardless of other Allows. BoolIfExists handles service-linked calls gracefully. The S3 command enables MFA Delete — now even a compromised admin credential cannot permanently delete versioned objects without the hardware second factor.

pitfalls: MFA only on console login, not on API — stolen access keys bypass console MFA; the policy condition covers both
No break-glass process: if the MFA device is lost with a Deny-all policy, you are locked out — document recovery
Ignoring Access Analyzer findings — the public bucket it flags today is the breach headline tomorrow
lessons.try_it: Attach the MFA-enforcement Deny to a test admin and confirm API calls fail without MFA.

lessons.title: EC2: Instances, AMIs, and Pricing Models
concepts: EC2 = virtual servers: you choose the AMI (OS image), instance type (CPU/RAM family), storage, and network placement
Pricing: On-Demand (no commitment), Spot (up to 90% off, interruptible), Savings Plans (commit $/hr for 1-3 years, up to 72% off), Reserved Instances
Instance families: general (M), compute (C), memory (R/X), storage (I/D), GPU (P/G) — match the family to the bottleneck
User data: bootstrap scripts at launch — install agents, join domains, pull config; bake AMIs for fast, consistent launches
Placement: spread across AZs for high availability; Auto Scaling replaces failed instances automatically

example.code:
# Launch with a hardened AMI + bootstrap
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --instance-type t3.medium --key-name ops-key \
  --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --subnet-id subnet-abcdef1234567890 \
  --user-data file://bootstrap.sh --tag-specifications \
  'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Env,Value=prod}]'
# Pricing rule: steady -> Savings Plan; spiky/fault-tolerant -> Spot.
example.walkthrough: The command launches from a known AMI into a specific subnet with a security group, tags the instance at birth, and bootstraps via user data. The pricing comment is the decision framework: steady-state workloads get Savings Plans, interruptible batch work gets Spot, and everything else starts On-Demand until the pattern is known.

pitfalls: Oversized instances to be safe — the most common EC2 waste; right-size with Compute Optimizer
Spot for stateful singletons — interruptions kill them; Spot is for fault-tolerant, checkpointed work
Manual console launches with no tags — untagged instances are unbillable mysteries; tag at launch
lessons.try_it: Run Compute Optimizer recommendations for one instance and identify whether it is over-provisioned.

lessons.title: Lambda: Serverless Functions
concepts: Lambda runs code without servers: upload the function, define the trigger (API Gateway, S3, EventBridge) — AWS runs it on events
Pricing: per request plus GB-seconds of execution — zero cost at idle; ideal for spiky, event-driven workloads
Limits: 15-minute max execution, 10GB memory, 512MB of /tmp — design functions small and stateless
Cold starts: first invocation initializes the runtime — keep packages lean; use provisioned concurrency only where latency demands it
Execution role: the function's IAM role defines what it can touch — least privilege applies to functions too

example.code:
# Deploy a function and wire an S3 trigger
aws lambda create-function --function-name thumbnailer \
  --runtime python3.12 --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lambda-s3-role \
  --handler index.handler --zip-file fileb://function.zip \
  --timeout 60 --memory-size 512
aws lambda add-permission --function-name thumbnailer \
  --statement-id s3-trigger --action lambda:InvokeFunction \
  --principal s3.amazonaws.com --source-arn arn:aws:s3:::uploads
example.walkthrough: The function gets a role (not keys), a 60-second timeout, and 512MB — sized to the job, not maxed. The permission grants S3 the right to invoke it, scoped to one bucket. This is the event-driven pattern: an upload lands, the function fires, a thumbnail appears — with zero idle cost between uploads.

pitfalls: Treating the 15-minute timeout as flexible — long jobs belong on Fargate or EC2, not Lambda
Huge deployment packages — cold starts balloon; trim dependencies
Function with AdministratorAccess role — a compromised function is a compromised account; scope the role
lessons.try_it: Create a Lambda that resizes an image on S3 upload and verify the trigger fires end-to-end.

lessons.title: Containers: ECS, Fargate, and EKS
concepts: Containers package app plus dependencies: consistent from laptop to production — images live in ECR (Elastic Container Registry)
ECS: AWS's orchestrator — task definitions run as services; simpler learning curve, deep AWS integration
Fargate: serverless containers — no EC2 to manage; pay per vCPU/memory-second; the default for most new ECS workloads
EKS: managed Kubernetes — choose it for existing K8s expertise, complex scheduling, or portability requirements
Decision rule: new container workload goes to ECS on Fargate; existing K8s investment goes to EKS; simplest path wins unless there is a reason

example.code:
# ECS on Fargate: the common path
aws ecs create-cluster --cluster-name orders --capacity-providers FARGATE
# Task definition: image from ECR, 0.5 vCPU / 1GB.
# Execution role: pulls the image + writes logs.
# Task role: the app's business permissions (separate!).
# Service: desiredCount=3 across 3 AZs, ALB target group, health check.
# EKS when: you already run Kubernetes and need its ecosystem.
example.walkthrough: The Fargate path removes server management: declare the task (image, CPU, memory, roles) and the service (count, AZ spread, load balancer), and ECS places and heals containers. The execution-role vs task-role split is the security design — one pulls images and writes logs, the other grants the app's business permissions.

pitfalls: EKS for a single simple service — Kubernetes operational overhead without the need; ECS/Fargate is simpler
latest tag in production — immutable tags (git SHA) or you cannot roll back reliably
Containers writing state to local disk — tasks are ephemeral; state goes to EBS, EFS, S3, or RDS
lessons.try_it: Push an image to ECR with a git-SHA tag and run it as a Fargate service with 2 tasks.

lessons.title: Elastic Beanstalk: Platform as a Service
concepts: Beanstalk: upload code, AWS provisions EC2, load balancer, and database — the fastest path from code to URL for standard web apps
You own the code and config; AWS owns the undifferentiated infra — a middle ground between Lambda and raw EC2
Environments: dev/test/prod as separate environments with CNAME swap for blue-green deployments
Customization via .ebextensions: config files for packages, commands, and resources the console does not expose
When not to use it: deep container or K8s needs (use ECS/EKS), or exotic architectures — Beanstalk optimizes for standard web tiers

example.code:
# Deploy a Python app
# 1. eb init -p python-3.11 my-app --region us-east-1
# 2. eb create prod-env --instance-type t3.small --min-instances 2
# 3. eb deploy   (zip upload -> rolling deploy)
# .ebextensions/01_packages.config:
# packages:
#   yum:
#     amazon-cloudwatch-agent: []
# Blue-green: eb swap prod-env-green prod-env-blue
example.walkthrough: Three commands take code to a load-balanced, multi-instance environment: init picks the platform, create provisions the environment, deploy pushes code with a rolling update. The .ebextensions file shows the escape hatch — the CloudWatch agent installed via config, not console clicks. Blue-green is a CNAME swap between two environments.

pitfalls: Console-click environments with no saved config — unreproducible; define everything in .ebextensions and saved configs
Single-instance environments for production — no HA; minimum 2 across AZs
Beanstalk for non-web workloads (batch, workers) — wrong tool; use Batch or Fargate
lessons.try_it: Deploy a sample app with eb create, then swap environments to practice blue-green.

lessons.title: Scaling and Load Balancing
concepts: Auto Scaling groups: maintain desired count, replace unhealthy instances, scale on metrics (CPU, request count, SQS depth)
Target tracking: keep CPU at 50% — the policy adds and removes instances automatically; simpler than step scaling
ALB (Application): HTTP/HTTPS routing, path and host rules, container targets — the default for web apps
NLB (Network): extreme performance, static IPs, TLS passthrough — for TCP/UDP and latency-sensitive workloads
Health checks: the load balancer's view of healthy — misconfigured health checks cause flapping and mass replacement

example.code:
# ASG: 2-6 instances, target 50% CPU
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg --min-size 2 --max-size 6 \
  --desired-capacity 2 --launch-template LaunchTemplateId=lt-0abc \
  --vpc-zone-identifier subnet-a,subnet-b,subnet-c
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --policy-name cpu50 \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration 'PredefinedMetricType=ASGAverageCPUUtilization,TargetValue=50.0'
# ALB rule: /api/* -> api-target-group; /* -> web-target-group
example.walkthrough: The ASG spans three AZs with a floor of 2 (HA) and ceiling of 6 (cost cap); the target-tracking policy holds CPU at 50% by adding or removing instances. The ALB rule shows content routing — API paths to one target group, everything else to another. Health checks on the target group decide what healthy means; get them wrong and the ASG churns instances.

pitfalls: min=max=1 — no HA and no scaling; the ASG is just an expensive instance
Health check on / (homepage) that depends on the database — a DB blip mass-kills the fleet; check a lightweight /health
Scaling on CPU for a queue-driven worker — scale on queue depth, not CPU
lessons.try_it: Load-test a sample ASG and watch target tracking add instances, then scale back in.

lessons.title: S3: Object Storage and Storage Classes
concepts: S3 stores objects (files) in buckets: 11 nines durability, unlimited scale, accessed via keys — the default for unstructured data
Standard: frequent access. Intelligent-Tiering: auto-moves between tiers for unknown patterns (small monitoring fee). Standard-IA / One Zone-IA: infrequent access, cheaper storage, retrieval fee
Glacier Instant Retrieval (ms), Glacier Flexible Retrieval (minutes-hours), Glacier Deep Archive (hours, cheapest) — the archive ladder
Choose by access pattern, not by price alone: retrieval fees punish the wrong tier — IA for backups touched rarely, Standard for hot data
Exam anchor: S3 is object storage; if the question says 'files needing a filesystem,' that is EFS, not S3

example.code:
# Upload with the right class from the start
aws s3 cp report.csv s3://app-reports/2026/ --storage-class STANDARD_IA
# Intelligent-Tiering for unpredictable access
aws s3 cp data/ s3://app-lake/raw/ --recursive \
  --storage-class INTELLIGENT_TIERING
# Rule of thumb: <1 access/month -> IA; yearly/legal hold -> Deep Archive.
example.walkthrough: The commands set the class at upload — but the real decision is the lifecycle policy (next lesson): data lands in Standard and ages into cheaper tiers automatically. The rule of thumb compresses the exam logic: hot stays Standard, warm goes IA, cold goes Glacier, frozen goes Deep Archive.

pitfalls: Everything in Standard forever — the most common S3 overspend; lifecycle it
Glacier for data retrieved weekly — retrieval fees exceed the storage savings
One Zone-IA for irreplaceable data — one AZ means one AZ failure from loss; it is for recreatable data
lessons.try_it: Classify 5 data types in a sample app (logs, backups, user uploads, reports, archives) into storage classes.

lessons.title: S3 Security and Data Protection
concepts: Block Public Access: the account/bucket-level kill switch — on by default; public buckets are almost always a misconfiguration
Bucket policies (resource-based) vs IAM policies (identity-based): use bucket policies for cross-account and public-access rules
Versioning: keeps every version of every object — the undo button for overwrites and deletes; pair with MFA Delete for critical data
Encryption: SSE-S3 (AWS-managed keys), SSE-KMS (your KMS keys, audit trail), SSE-C (your keys) — encrypt everything, default to SSE-S3 or KMS
Presigned URLs: time-limited direct access to private objects — the app vends URLs, users download straight from S3

example.code:
# Lock it down: block public, version, encrypt by default
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket app-reports \
  --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket app-reports \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket app-reports \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"aws:kms"}}]}'
# Share privately: presigned URL valid 1 hour
aws s3 presign s3://app-reports/q3.pdf --expires-in 3600
example.walkthrough: The three commands are the secure-bucket baseline: no public access in any form, versioning on, KMS encryption by default. The presign command shows the sharing pattern — private bucket, temporary URL — which is how you share without making anything public. This sequence answers half the S3 security questions on the exam.

pitfalls: Public bucket for a 'temporary' share — temporary becomes permanent; use presigned URLs
Versioning off on critical buckets — ransomware or a bad script deletes the only copy
Bucket policy with Principal: * and no conditions — audit every wildcard principal
lessons.try_it: Audit one bucket: check public access block, versioning, and default encryption; fix what is missing.

lessons.title: S3 Lifecycle and Replication
concepts: Lifecycle policies: transition objects between classes on age (Standard -> IA at 30 days -> Glacier at 90), then expire — automation beats good intentions
Expiration: delete old versions, incomplete multipart uploads, and logs past retention — storage you do not need is waste
CRR (cross-region replication): compliance, disaster recovery, and latency — copies new objects to another region automatically
SRR (same-region replication): aggregate logs into one bucket, or separate production data for analytics
Replication needs versioning on both buckets; RTC (replication time control) gives a 15-minute SLA for critical data

example.walkthrough: The rule reads as a data-aging policy: logs sit in Standard for 30 days (hot analysis window), cool to IA, freeze in Glacier at 90 days, and disappear at a year per retention. Old versions get 30 days of undo. Write the lifecycle when you create the bucket — retrofitting it later means paying Standard prices until you do.

pitfalls: Lifecycle on the wrong prefix — Filter scoping mistakes age out (or never age) the wrong data
No expiration for old versions — versioning without expiry grows storage forever
CRR without versioning enabled — replication silently does nothing
lessons.try_it: Write a lifecycle policy for a logs bucket: 30/90/365 aging plus old-version expiry.

lessons.title: EBS, EFS, and Instance Store
concepts: EBS: block storage for one EC2 instance — like a virtual hard drive; gp3 (general), io2 (high IOPS), st1/sc1 (throughput/cold HDD)
EBS snapshots: point-in-time backups to S3 — the basis for AMIs, disaster recovery, and volume migration
EFS: managed NFS file system — shared across many instances and AZs; for 'shared file storage' questions, EFS is the answer
Instance store: ephemeral NVMe on the host — blazing fast, gone when the instance stops; for caches and temp data only
Decision: one instance needs a disk -> EBS; many instances share files -> EFS; scratch speed -> instance store; objects -> S3

example.code:
# Snapshot before risky changes (your undo button)
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --description "pre-upgrade $(date +%F)"
# EFS: mount on many instances
# sudo mount -t efs fs-0123456789abcdef0:/ /mnt/shared
# Decision card:
# boot disk -> EBS gp3 | database -> EBS io2 | shared uploads -> EFS
# build cache -> instance store | backups -> S3
example.walkthrough: The snapshot command is operational hygiene: snapshot before upgrades, before migrations, before anything risky — restore is a new volume from the snapshot. The decision card compresses the exam logic: the question's keywords (one instance, shared files, ephemeral speed, objects) map directly to EBS, EFS, instance store, S3.

pitfalls: EBS for shared storage — it attaches to one instance; sharing needs EFS
Irreplaceable data on instance store — a stop/terminate wipes it; ephemeral means ephemeral
No snapshots before changes — the one time you skip it is the one time you need it
lessons.try_it: For a WordPress-on-EC2 design, assign each storage need (OS disk, uploads, backups) to EBS/EFS/S3.

lessons.title: Hybrid Storage: Gateway, DataSync, Transfer
concepts: Storage Gateway: on-prem appliance (VM or hardware) presenting S3, EBS snapshots, or tape to local apps — the hybrid bridge
Gateway modes: S3 File Gateway (NFS/SMB to S3), Volume Gateway (iSCSI volumes cached/stored), Tape Gateway (VTL to Glacier)
DataSync: managed online migration and sync — on-prem to S3/EFS/FSx, with scheduling, verification, and bandwidth controls
Transfer Family: managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP into S3 or EFS — for partners and legacy workflows that speak file-transfer protocols
Exam split: migrate data online -> DataSync; keep on-prem apps with cloud backend -> Storage Gateway; SFTP partner feeds -> Transfer Family

example.code:
# DataSync: 50TB file server -> S3, scheduled nightly
aws datasync create-task --source-location-arn arn:aws:datasync:...:location/loc-0abc \
  --destination-location-arn arn:aws:datasync:...:location/loc-0def \
  --schedule '{"ScheduleExpression": "cron(0 2 * * ? *)"}'
# Transfer Family: partner SFTP drop -> S3
aws transfer create-server --protocols SFTP --endpoint-type PUBLIC \
  --identity-provider-type SERVICE_MANAGED
example.walkthrough: DataSync is the managed mover: point it at source and destination, schedule it, and it handles deltas, verification, and throttling. Transfer Family is the protocol adapter: partners keep using SFTP while files land in S3. The exam distinction is crisp — migration vs ongoing-protocol vs hybrid-appliance.

pitfalls: Storage Gateway for a one-time migration — it is for ongoing hybrid, not moves; use DataSync
Sneakernet for 500GB — the Snow family starts making sense around tens of TB, not GB
Transfer Family for app-to-app APIs — it is a file-transfer protocol service, not an API gateway
lessons.try_it: A partner sends nightly CSVs via SFTP: design the landing (Transfer Family -> S3 -> trigger) on paper.

lessons.title: RDS: Managed Relational Databases
concepts: RDS = managed relational: AWS handles patching, backups, and failover for MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server
Multi-AZ: synchronous standby in another AZ, automatic failover — for high availability, not performance
Read replicas: asynchronous copies for read scaling — for performance, not failover (unless promoted)
Automated backups: point-in-time recovery within the retention window (up to 35 days); snapshots are manual and permanent
The exam split: Multi-AZ = availability (failover), Read Replica = performance (scale reads) — never mix them up

example.code:
# Production-grade RDS: Multi-AZ + replica + backups
aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large --engine postgres \
  --multi-az --backup-retention-period 7 --storage-encrypted
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier orders-rr --source-db-instance-identifier orders-db
# Failover is automatic; replicas take read traffic.
example.walkthrough: The commands build the standard production shape: Multi-AZ for automatic failover, encrypted storage, 7-day point-in-time recovery, plus a read replica for read scaling. The comment states the exam-critical distinction — failover and read scaling are different features solving different problems.

pitfalls: Multi-AZ for read scaling — it is a standby, not a reader; replicas scale reads
No automated backups because snapshots exist — snapshots are manual; PITR needs automated backups
Single-AZ production databases — one AZ failure is a full outage
lessons.try_it: Design an RDS setup for a production orders DB: state the HA and read-scaling choices.

lessons.title: Aurora: Cloud-Native Relational
concepts: Aurora: AWS's cloud-native MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible engine — the default choice for new relational workloads
Cluster architecture: storage auto-scales to 128TB, replicated 6 ways across 3 AZs; compute and storage scale independently
Reader endpoints: load-balance reads across up to 15 replicas with ~ms replica lag
Aurora Global Database: cross-region reads with <1s replication lag, plus managed disaster recovery failover
Aurora Serverless v2: scales capacity in fine increments for variable workloads — pay for what you use

example.code:
# Aurora cluster: writer + 2 readers, Global Database for DR
aws rds create-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier app-aurora \
  --engine aurora-postgresql --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password <secret> --storage-encrypted
# Readers: create-db-instance --db-cluster-identifier app-aurora (x2)
# Global: create-global-cluster spanning us-east-1 + eu-west-1
# Serverless v2: set ServerlessV2ScalingConfiguration Min/MaxCapacity.
example.walkthrough: The cluster separates concerns: one writer endpoint, a reader endpoint spreading load, storage that grows itself. Global Database adds the cross-region story with sub-second lag. Serverless v2 covers the spiky case — the exam loves asking when Serverless v2 beats provisioned (variable, unpredictable workloads).

pitfalls: Aurora for a tiny dev database — overkill; RDS or Serverless v2 fits better
Expecting Multi-AZ-style failover config — Aurora's storage-layer replication makes failover near-instant and automatic
Cross-region reads from the writer endpoint — use the reader endpoint or Global Database readers
lessons.try_it: Choose Aurora vs RDS for: a global SaaS app, a small internal tool, a spiky analytics DB.

lessons.title: DynamoDB: NoSQL Key-Value
concepts: DynamoDB: serverless NoSQL key-value — single-digit ms at any scale, no servers to manage
Keys: partition key (required) for distribution; optional sort key for range queries — design access patterns first, tables second
Capacity: on-demand (pay per request, spiky/unknown) vs provisioned (predictable, cheaper with auto scaling)
DAX: in-memory cache for DynamoDB — microsecond reads for read-heavy hot keys
Global Tables: multi-region active-active replication — for global apps needing local reads and writes

example.code:
# On-demand table for spiky traffic
aws dynamodb create-table --table-name sessions \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=userId,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=userId,KeyType=HASH \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST
# Hot keys + heavy reads? Add DAX. Global app? Global Tables.
# Point-in-time recovery: --point-in-time-recovery-specification PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled=true
example.walkthrough: The table is on-demand — no capacity planning for spiky session traffic — with a simple partition key. The comments layer the options: DAX for hot-key caching, Global Tables for multi-region, PITR for recovery. The exam pattern: 'millions of requests, single-digit ms, no servers' is always DynamoDB.

pitfalls: Relational modeling in DynamoDB (joins via scans) — design access patterns first; scans do not scale
Provisioned without auto scaling for spiky traffic — throttling; use on-demand or auto scaling
Hot partition key (all writes to one key) — throttles the partition; distribute the key space
lessons.try_it: Design a DynamoDB key schema for user sessions: pick partition/sort keys and justify them.

lessons.title: ElastiCache and Redshift
concepts: ElastiCache: managed Redis or Memcached — the caching layer that takes read pressure off the database
Redis: rich data structures, persistence, pub/sub — the default choice; Memcached: simple, multithreaded, for plain key-value caching
Redshift: petabyte-scale data warehouse — columnar storage, massive parallel processing for analytics SQL
Redshift Serverless: no cluster to size — for intermittent analytics workloads
Exam split: cache frequent DB reads -> ElastiCache; run complex analytics over huge data -> Redshift; transactional app data -> RDS/Aurora/DynamoDB

example.code:
# Redis cluster for session + query caching
aws elasticache create-replication-group \
  --replication-group-id app-cache --engine redis \
  --cache-node-type cache.r6g.large --num-cache-clusters 2
# App pattern: cache-aside — check Redis, on miss query DB and populate.
# Redshift Serverless for the analytics team: no sizing, pay per query.
example.walkthrough: The Redis replication group gives a primary plus replica for the cache layer; the app uses cache-aside — check cache, miss goes to the database and repopulates. Redshift Serverless covers analytics without cluster sizing. The exam split in the comment is the decision tree: cache, warehouse, or transactional store.

pitfalls: ElastiCache as the system of record — it is a cache; data loss is acceptable by design
Redshift for transactional workloads — it is OLAP, not OLTP; row-level transactions belong in RDS
No TTL on cached items — stale data served forever; set expirations
lessons.try_it: Place a caching layer in front of a slow product-catalog query: choose Redis vs Memcached and set TTLs.

lessons.title: DMS and Choosing the Database
concepts: DMS (Database Migration Service): replicate databases with minimal downtime — homogeneous (Oracle to Oracle) or heterogeneous (Oracle to Aurora)
SCT (Schema Conversion Tool): converts schemas and stored procedures for heterogeneous migrations — DMS moves data, SCT converts schema
Migration pattern: full load plus ongoing CDC (change data capture) — cut over when the replica lag hits zero
Choosing: relational + joins + transactions -> RDS/Aurora; key-value + massive scale -> DynamoDB; cache -> ElastiCache; analytics -> Redshift
Exam anchor: 'migrate database with minimal downtime' is DMS; 'Oracle to Aurora' is DMS plus SCT

example.code:
# DMS: Oracle -> Aurora PostgreSQL, minimal downtime
# 1. SCT: convert schema, assess stored procedures
# 2. DMS task: full load + CDC (ongoing replication)
#    --migration-type full-load-and-cdc
# 3. Validate row counts + checksums
# 4. Cut over in the maintenance window when lag ~ 0
# Choosing card: joins/txns->Aurora | kv/scale->DynamoDB |
# cache->ElastiCache | analytics->Redshift
example.walkthrough: The four steps are the heterogeneous migration playbook: SCT converts what DMS cannot, the DMS task keeps replicating changes until cutover, validation proves fidelity, and the cutover happens when lag is zero. The choosing card compresses the database decision to one line per workload shape.

pitfalls: DMS without SCT for Oracle to Aurora — the data moves, the stored procedures do not convert themselves
Cutover without validation — row counts and checksums first, traffic second
Big-bang migration with downtime — CDC exists so you do not need it
lessons.try_it: Plan a migration: on-prem MySQL to Aurora with a 2-hour cutover window — list the DMS steps.

lessons.title: VPC: Your Private Cloud
concepts: VPC: your isolated network in AWS — you define the CIDR (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16), subnets, and routing
Subnets: public (route to an Internet Gateway) vs private (no direct internet) — web tier public, app/data tiers private
Route tables: control where traffic goes per subnet — the public table points 0.0.0.0/0 at the IGW
NAT gateway: lets private subnets reach the internet (updates, patches) without being reachable from it — in each AZ for HA
Exam anchor: public subnet = has IGW route; private = does not. NAT goes in the public subnet, serving the private ones

example.code:
# 3-tier VPC sketch (10.0.0.0/16)
# Public subnets:  10.0.1.0/24 (a), 10.0.2.0/24 (b) -> IGW route
# Private (app):   10.0.11.0/24 (a), 10.0.12.0/24 (b) -> NAT route
# Private (data):  10.0.21.0/24 (a), 10.0.22.0/24 (b) -> no internet route
# ALB in public, EC2 in app-private, RDS in data-private.
# NAT gateway in each public subnet (AZ HA).
example.walkthrough: The sketch is the canonical 3-tier VPC: the ALB faces the internet from public subnets, app servers hide in private subnets reaching out via NAT, and the database sits in subnets with no internet route at all. Every tier's route table tells the story — follow the 0.0.0.0/0 route to see what each tier can reach.

pitfalls: One big public subnet for everything — the database is internet-routable; tier it
Single NAT gateway for all AZs — AZ failure kills outbound for every private subnet; one per AZ
Overlapping CIDRs with on-prem — VPN/Direct Connect routing breaks; plan CIDRs before peering
lessons.try_it: Draw a 3-tier VPC for a web app: label subnets, route tables, IGW, and NAT placement.

lessons.title: Security Groups vs NACLs
concepts: Security groups: stateful instance-level firewalls — allow rules only; return traffic is automatic; evaluated per ENI
NACLs: stateless subnet-level — allow AND deny rules, numbered lowest-first; return traffic needs explicit rules
Default posture: use security groups for nearly everything; NACLs for coarse subnet-level guardrails (e.g., block a malicious IP at the subnet)
Security group referencing: allow app-tier SG from web-tier SG (not from IPs) — the group membership becomes the rule
Exam trap: 'stateless' is NACL; 'stateful' is security group. NACLs need ephemeral-port rules for return traffic

example.code:
# Web tier SG: allow 443 from 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-web \
  --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
# App tier SG: allow 8080 ONLY from the web tier SG (not IPs)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-app \
  --protocol tcp --port 8080 --source-group sg-web
# NACL: deny a malicious IP at the subnet (rule 90, before allow-all 100*)
example.walkthrough: The app-tier rule shows the best practice: source-group referencing instead of CIDRs — when web instances change IPs, the rule still works because it follows the group. The NACL example shows its niche: a numbered deny for a bad actor at the subnet edge, evaluated before the allow-all.

pitfalls: Opening 0.0.0.0/0 to the database port 'temporarily' — temporary becomes permanent; scope it
NACL allow inbound without outbound ephemeral rules — return traffic drops; NACLs are stateless
IP-based rules between tiers — brittle; reference security groups instead
lessons.try_it: Write the SG rules for web->app->db tiers using group references, then add a NACL deny for a bad IP.

lessons.title: Connecting Networks
concepts: VPC peering: private 1:1 connection between VPCs — non-transitive (A-B and B-C does not give A-C)
Transit Gateway: the hub — connect VPCs and on-prem through one gateway; transitive routing, the answer for many-VPC estates
Site-to-Site VPN: encrypted tunnel over the internet — fast to set up, variable latency; for steady high-throughput, use Direct Connect
Direct Connect: dedicated private fiber to AWS — consistent bandwidth, lower data-transfer pricing; takes weeks to provision
PrivateLink: private connectivity to AWS services (or SaaS) without internet — S3/DynamoDB via gateway endpoints (free), others via interface endpoints

example.code:
# Decision card:
# 2 VPCs, simple            -> VPC peering
# 10 VPCs + on-prem hub     -> Transit Gateway
# Quick encrypted link      -> Site-to-Site VPN (hours)
# Steady 5 Gbps + compliance-> Direct Connect (weeks)
# Private S3 from VPC       -> Gateway endpoint (free, no NAT)
# SaaS API privately        -> PrivateLink interface endpoint
example.walkthrough: The decision card is the exam: count the networks and the constraints. Two VPCs is peering; many networks is Transit Gateway; speed of setup is VPN; consistent throughput is Direct Connect; private service access is PrivateLink. S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints are free — traffic to S3 never needs NAT.

pitfalls: Peering for 20 VPCs — full mesh is 190 peerings; use Transit Gateway
VPN for steady 10 Gbps — variable internet latency; Direct Connect fits
S3 traffic through NAT — costs money and bandwidth; gateway endpoints are free
lessons.try_it: Choose the connection for: 2 VPCs, 12 VPCs plus on-prem, S3 privately, 8 Gbps steady.

lessons.title: Route 53 and CloudFront
concepts: Route 53: AWS DNS — hosted zones, routing policies (simple, weighted, latency-based, failover, geolocation)
Failover routing: health-check the primary, route to secondary on failure — DNS-level disaster recovery
CloudFront: global CDN — caches content at edge locations, cutting latency and origin load
Origins: S3, ALB, EC2 — with Origin Access Control so S3 stays private while CloudFront serves publicly
Exam pair: 'global users, low latency, static content' is CloudFront; 'DNS failover between regions' is Route 53

example.code:
# Failover DNS: primary + secondary with health checks
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 \
  --change-batch '{"Changes":[{"Action":"CREATE","ResourceRecordSet":{
  "Name":"app.example.com","Type":"A","SetIdentifier":"primary",
  "Failover":"PRIMARY","HealthCheckId":"hc-abc",
  "AliasTarget":{"DNSName":"alb-1...elb.amazonaws.com"}}}]}'
# CloudFront: S3 origin + OAC, cache behaviors by path (/static/* long TTL).
example.walkthrough: The Route 53 record shows DNS failover mechanics: the PRIMARY record is served while its health check passes; on failure, traffic shifts to SECONDARY. CloudFront's piece is the edge cache with OAC — private S3 origin, public edge. Together they are the global-availability answer: CDN for latency, DNS failover for region loss.

pitfalls: Single-region DNS with no health checks — region failure means manual DNS edits under pressure
CloudFront in front of a private S3 without OAC — 403s; the origin must trust CloudFront
No cache behaviors — one TTL for everything; static assets deserve long TTLs, APIs short
lessons.try_it: Design failover for an app in 2 regions: Route 53 records, health checks, and CloudFront origin strategy.

lessons.title: Designing a Secure VPC
concepts: Defense in depth: NACLs at subnet edges, security groups at instances, WAF at the ALB, GuardDuty watching — layers, not one wall
Bastion hosts are legacy: SSM Session Manager gives shell access with IAM auth and full audit — no inbound SSH, no keys
VPC endpoints: reach S3/DynamoDB/SSM privately — data-tier subnets with no internet route still get AWS services
Flow Logs: capture IP traffic metadata for forensics — the answer to 'who talked to the database at 2 AM'
3-tier recap: ALB public, app private, data isolated — each tier's security group only trusts the tier above

example.code:
# No bastion: SSM Session Manager
aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0
# (Instance needs SSM agent + instance profile; SG needs NO ssh rule.)
# Flow Logs -> CloudWatch: who talked to whom, when.
aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type VPC --resource-ids vpc-0abc \
  --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type cloud-watch-logs \
  --log-group-name vpc-flow-logs
# WAF on the ALB: block SQLi/XSS patterns at the edge.
example.walkthrough: Session Manager removes the two worst bastion properties — inbound SSH and long-lived keys — replacing them with IAM-authenticated, fully logged sessions. Flow Logs are the forensic backstop: every connection attempt recorded. The WAF at the ALB filters web attacks before they reach the app. Layers, each doing its job.

pitfalls: Bastion with 0.0.0.0/0 SSH — the internet's favorite brute-force target; use Session Manager
No Flow Logs — incidents become unsolvable mysteries; enable them before you need them
App tier reaching the internet directly — updates via NAT or endpoints, never direct routes
lessons.try_it: Harden a sample VPC: replace bastion SSH with Session Manager, enable Flow Logs, add WAF to the ALB.

lessons.title: CloudWatch: Metrics, Alarms, and Logs
concepts: CloudWatch metrics: time-series data (CPU, latency, custom business metrics) — the numbers you graph and alarm on
Alarms: threshold plus evaluation periods plus action (SNS notify, Auto Scaling, EC2 action) — monitoring that does something
CloudWatch Logs: centralized log ingestion; Logs Insights queries it with a SQL-like language for forensics
Dashboards: one pane for metrics, alarms, and log widgets — the NOC view
Composite alarms and anomaly detection: alarm on 'unusual' instead of fixed thresholds for spiky metrics

example.code:
# Alarm: CPU > 80% for 5 min -> notify + scale
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name web-cpu-high \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Average --period 60 --evaluation-periods 5 \
  --threshold 80 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:ops-alerts
# Logs Insights: find the 500s
# fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/
# | stats count() by bin(5m)
example.walkthrough: The alarm command shows the anatomy: metric, statistic, period, evaluation windows, threshold, and the action (SNS). The Logs Insights query is the forensic companion — when the alarm fires, this finds the errors in the window. Metrics tell you something is wrong; logs tell you what.

pitfalls: Alarming on a single datapoint — noise; use evaluation periods
No action on the alarm — an alarm nobody acts on is a dashboard decoration; wire SNS/Auto Scaling
Logs without retention policy — infinite retention is infinite cost; set it
lessons.try_it: Create one alarm with an SNS action and one Logs Insights query for your app's errors.

lessons.title: CloudTrail vs Config
concepts: CloudTrail: WHO did WHAT via the API — every console click and CLI call logged; the audit trail for actions
Config: WHAT does the infrastructure look like — resource inventory plus configuration history and compliance rules
The exam split: 'who changed the security group' is CloudTrail; 'is the bucket encrypted right now' is Config
Config rules: continuous compliance (e.g., 'all EBS volumes encrypted') with auto-remediation via SSM
CloudTrail Lake / S3 archival: keep the trail for years for compliance; encrypt the trail bucket

example.code:
# Who opened the security group? (CloudTrail)
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress \
  --start-time 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z
# Is every EBS volume encrypted? (Config rule)
aws configservice put-config-rule --config-rule \
  '{"ConfigRuleName":"ebs-encrypted","Source":{"Owner":"AWS","SourceIdentifier":"ENCRYPTED_VOLUMES"}}'
example.walkthrough: The two commands are the two questions: lookup-events answers who-did-what (the API history), put-config-rule answers what-is-the-state (continuous compliance). On the exam, map the question's verb — 'who/which action' is Trail, 'is it compliant' is Config.

pitfalls: CloudTrail off in a region — the attacker’s first move is deleting the trail; enable org-wide with log file validation
Config without rules — inventory without compliance is just a list
Confusing the two on the exam — memorize: Trail = actions, Config = state
lessons.try_it: Enable a Config rule for encrypted volumes and query CloudTrail for one recent API action.

lessons.title: EventBridge and SNS
concepts: EventBridge: the event bus — AWS services emit events; rules route them to targets (Lambda, Step Functions, SNS)
Scheduled events: cron/rate triggers — the serverless cron for Lambda (replaces cron on a box)
SNS: pub/sub notifications — one message fans out to email, SMS, Lambda, SQS, mobile push
SNS vs SQS: SNS pushes to many subscribers (fan-out); SQS queues for one consumer to pull (decoupling) — often paired: SNS -> SQS
Event-driven pattern: S3 upload -> EventBridge -> Lambda thumbnailer + SNS notify — no polling anywhere

example.code:
# Nightly report: EventBridge cron -> Lambda
aws events put-rule --name nightly-report \
  --schedule-expression 'cron(0 6 * * ? *)'
aws events put-targets --rule nightly-report \
  --targets '[{"Id":"1","Arn":"arn:aws:lambda:...:function:report"}]'
# Fan-out: SNS topic -> email + SMS + Lambda
aws sns create-topic --name deploys
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:...:deploys \
  --protocol email --notification-endpoint ops@example.com
example.walkthrough: The EventBridge rule is serverless cron — no server, no crontab to maintain. The SNS topic shows fan-out: one publish reaches email, SMS, and Lambda simultaneously. The exam pairing to memorize: events-and-scheduling is EventBridge, human-and-multi-target notification is SNS.

pitfalls: Polling SQS in a loop from cron on EC2 — EventBridge schedules and Lambda reacts; no servers
SNS for guaranteed ordered delivery — SNS is at-least-once and unordered; SQS FIFO is the ordered queue
One SNS topic for everything — topics are cheap; separate by purpose for sane subscriptions
lessons.try_it: Build an event flow: S3 upload triggers Lambda via EventBridge and notifies via SNS.

lessons.title: X-Ray and Health Dashboards
concepts: X-Ray: distributed tracing — follow a request across ALB, Lambda, DynamoDB; find which hop is slow
Service maps: X-Ray draws the architecture from traces — the living diagram of your system
Sampling: trace 1 in 100 normally, 100% during incidents — full tracing at scale is expensive
Service Health Dashboard: AWS's status page — is the region having an issue, or is it you?
Personal Health Dashboard: YOUR account's events — scheduled maintenance, your resources affected — wire it to EventBridge for alerts

example.code:
# X-Ray: instrument the SDK (one line per service)
# from aws_xray_sdk.core import xray_recorder
# xray_recorder.capture('process')  # wraps the function
# Then: service map shows ALB -> Lambda (40ms) -> DynamoDB (900ms).
# The 900ms hop is the fix — not the Lambda, not the ALB.
# Personal Health -> EventBridge rule -> SNS: 'your RDS has
# scheduled maintenance Friday' -> alert before it surprises you.
example.walkthrough: X-Ray's value is attribution: the trace shows exactly which hop owns the latency — without it, teams optimize the wrong service. The Health dashboards answer the first incident question: check Personal Health before debugging your code; if AWS is impaired, your deploy did not cause it.

pitfalls: Debugging latency without traces — guessing which service is slow; trace first
Ignoring Personal Health — scheduled maintenance surprises become incidents
100% X-Ray sampling in production — cost and overhead; sample, then raise during incidents
lessons.try_it: Enable X-Ray on one Lambda and read its service map; check Personal Health for upcoming events.

lessons.title: Building an Observability Strategy
concepts: The three pillars: metrics (numbers), logs (events), traces (request paths) — you need all three; each answers different questions
Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation — alarm on these four before anything exotic
Runbooks linked to alarms: every alarm pages with a link to the fix steps — an alarm without a runbook is anxiety
Separate signal from noise: page on symptoms (checkout failing), ticket on causes (CPU high) — paging on CPU wakes people for non-incidents
Review cadence: weekly alarm review — tune thresholds, delete dead alarms, add missing coverage

example.code:
# Strategy checklist:
# [ ] Golden-signal alarms on every critical path (paged)
# [ ] Logs centralized with retention + Insights queries saved
# [ ] Traces on the request path (X-Ray, sampled)
# [ ] Every alarm links a runbook; every runbook has an owner
# [ ] CloudTrail org-wide + Config rules for compliance
# [ ] Personal Health -> EventBridge -> SNS alerts
example.walkthrough: The checklist is the strategy in one page: paged alarms on what users feel, logs and traces for diagnosis, audit and compliance underneath, runbooks attached to everything. If an alarm fires and nobody knows what to do, the monitoring is incomplete — the runbook link is part of the alarm.

pitfalls: Monitoring everything equally — alert fatigue; tier by user impact
Alarms without owners — nobody tunes them, everybody ignores them
Only infrastructure metrics — business metrics (orders/min) catch what CPU never will
lessons.try_it: Grade your current monitoring against the checklist; fix the biggest gap first.

lessons.title: Cloud Pricing Models and TCO
concepts: Pay-as-you-go: no upfront, pay per second/hour/GB — the default; trade capex for opex
Savings Plans: commit to $/hour for 1-3 years, save up to 72% — flexible across instance families and regions
Reserved Instances: commit to a specific instance type — less flexible than Savings Plans, similar discounts
Spot: spare capacity up to 90% off — for fault-tolerant work only
TCO: compare 3-year on-prem (hardware, power, staff, refresh) vs cloud — the Pricing Calculator models it; include people cost, not just servers

example.code:
# Pricing Calculator inputs for a TCO comparison:
# - 50 EC2 (16 vCPU, 64GB) 3yr, 10TB S3 Standard, 5TB/mo transfer
# - Compare: On-Demand vs 3yr Savings Plan vs on-prem refresh
# Rule: steady 24/7 -> Savings Plan; variable -> On-Demand;
# fault-tolerant batch -> Spot. Revisit quarterly.
example.walkthrough: The calculator only helps with honest inputs: model the real fleet, the real storage, the real transfer — then compare the three purchase options side by side. The rule of thumb assigns each workload shape to its cheapest correct model; the quarterly revisit catches drift as workloads change.

pitfalls: On-Demand for steady 24/7 workloads — the most common overspend; commit with Savings Plans
TCO comparing only hardware — people, power, and refresh cycles are half the on-prem cost
Spot for production databases — interruptions are data loss; Spot is for disposable work
lessons.try_it: Classify 5 workloads by shape (steady/variable/batch) and assign each a pricing model.

lessons.title: Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Anomaly Detection
concepts: Cost Explorer: visualize spend by service, account, tag — find the spike, then the cause; rightsizing recommendations included
AWS Budgets: alert (or act) at thresholds — actual, forecasted, and RI/Savings Plan utilization budgets
Cost Anomaly Detection: ML on your spend — flags unusual patterns without manual thresholds
The workflow: Anomaly Detection catches it, Cost Explorer explains it, Budgets prevent the surprise next time
Tag discipline makes all of this work: untagged spend is unexplainable spend

example.code:
# Budget: alert at 80% forecasted, act at 100%
aws budgets create-budget --account-id 123456789012 --budget \
  '{"BudgetName":"monthly","BudgetLimit":{"Amount":"5000","Unit":"USD"},"TimeUnit":"MONTHLY","BudgetType":"COST"}' \
  --notifications-with-subscribers '[{"Notification":{"NotificationType":"FORECASTED","ComparisonOperator":"GREATER_THAN","Threshold":80},"Subscribers":[{"SubscriptionType":"EMAIL","Address":"finops@example.com"}]}]'
# Anomaly Detection: create a monitor, get alerted on the weird — not on fixed lines.
example.walkthrough: The budget alerts on forecasted spend — you hear about the overrun before the month ends, not after. Anomaly Detection covers what fixed thresholds miss: the new-service spike, the region you never use suddenly billing. Together they are the early-warning system; Cost Explorer is the investigation tool.

pitfalls: Budgets with no subscribers — alerts nobody reads; route to the team that can act
Fixed thresholds only — slow ramps never trip them; anomaly detection catches the shape
Investigating without tags — 'EC2 $8k' explains nothing; tag by team/project
lessons.try_it: Create a forecasted budget with an 80% alert and enable an anomaly monitor.

lessons.title: Organizations and Consolidated Billing
concepts: Organizations: manage multiple accounts — one payer, linked accounts; volume discounts aggregate across the estate
OUs (organizational units): group accounts (prod, dev, security) — policies and budgets attach at the OU level
SCPs (service control policies): guardrails on what accounts can do — e.g., deny leaving the org, deny unencrypted volumes
Consolidated billing: one bill, combined usage tiers — the 10th TB is cheaper because all accounts' usage counts together
Exam anchor: multi-account governance is Organizations + SCPs; the question saying 'centrally control' is SCPs

example.code:
# Structure:
# Root
# ├── Security OU (audit, log-archive accounts)
# ├── Prod OU (SCP: deny ec2:TerminateInstances on prod DBs)
# └── Dev OU  (SCP: deny expensive instance types)
# SCP example: deny leaving the organization
# {"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Deny",
#   "Action":"organizations:LeaveOrganization","Resource":"*"}]}
# Consolidated billing: automatic — usage pools across linked accounts.
example.walkthrough: The OU tree is the governance map: security accounts isolated, prod and dev under different guardrails, SCPs enforcing the non-negotiables. The leave-organization deny is the classic — it prevents an account (and its bill) from walking away. Consolidated billing then makes the whole estate cheaper than the sum of its accounts.

pitfalls: One account for everything — no blast-radius isolation, no per-team billing
SCPs as the only control — SCPs are guardrails (deny), not grants; identity policies still grant
No log-archive account — security logs in the workload account can be tampered with
lessons.try_it: Sketch an OU structure for 3 teams plus security, with one SCP per OU.

lessons.title: Cost Allocation and the CUR
concepts: Cost allocation tags: tag resources (Team, Project, Env) — activate the tags in billing, then slice spend by tag
Tag policies: enforce required tags via Organizations — untagged resources get flagged, not billed mysteriously
CUR (Cost and Usage Report): the detailed CSV/Parquet in S3 — every charge, every hour; the source of truth for FinOps
Query the CUR with Athena: SQL over the detailed bill — 'which team spent what on data transfer last Tuesday'
Chargeback/showback: allocate the bill to teams by tag — the accountability loop that actually changes behavior

example.code:
-- Athena over the CUR: top 10 untagged costs last month
SELECT line_item_product_code, SUM(line_item_unblended_cost) AS cost
FROM cur_db.cur_table
WHERE month = '2026-09'
  AND line_item_unblended_cost > 0
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY cost DESC LIMIT 10;
-- Tag policy: require Team + Project on EC2/RDS at creation.
-- Activate user-defined tags in Billing console -> Cost allocation tags.
example.walkthrough: The Athena query turns the CUR from an unreadable dump into answers — top costs by service, filterable by tag, down to the hour. Tag policies close the loop at creation: resources arrive tagged or flagged. Without tags, the CUR is precise but meaningless; with them, every dollar has an owner.

pitfalls: User-defined tags never activated — they exist on resources but not in billing; activate them
CUR never enabled — the detailed data you need for the one hard question does not exist retroactively
No tag enforcement — 40% untagged spend makes chargeback fiction
lessons.try_it: Activate two cost allocation tags and write one Athena query slicing spend by team.

lessons.title: Support Plans and Cost Optimization
concepts: Support tiers: Basic (free), Developer (business hours, $29+), Business (24/7, $100+), Enterprise On-Ramp ($5,500+), Enterprise ($15k+, TAM)
Choose by need: production workloads get Business minimum (24/7 + IEM); Enterprise adds the TAM and Concierge team
Compute Optimizer: rightsizing recommendations for EC2, Lambda, EBS — the free 'you are over-provisioned' report
Trusted Advisor cost checks: idle resources, unassociated EIPs, old snapshots — the free waste finder
The optimization loop: measure (Cost Explorer) -> right-size (Compute Optimizer) -> commit (Savings Plans) -> govern (Budgets)

example.code:
# Monthly FinOps loop (calendar it):
# 1. Cost Explorer: top 5 services, MoM delta
# 2. Trusted Advisor: cost checks — act on red/yellow
# 3. Compute Optimizer: apply rightsizing (dev first)
# 4. Savings Plans: cover the steady baseline
# 5. Budgets: confirm alerts route to owners
# Support: prod workloads -> Business (24/7); regulated/large -> Enterprise.
example.walkthrough: The loop is the discipline: monthly, in order, owned by someone. Trusted Advisor finds the waste, Compute Optimizer sizes it right, Savings Plans price the steady remainder, Budgets guard the future. The support-plan line is the exam fact plus the operational truth — production without 24/7 support is a gamble.

pitfalls: Enterprise support for a dev account — $15k for a TAM nobody calls; match tier to need
One-time optimization project — waste regrows; the loop must be monthly
Ignoring Trusted Advisor reds — free findings, ignored
lessons.try_it: Run Trusted Advisor cost checks and act on the top red finding.

lessons.title: The Well-Architected Framework
concepts: Six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability — the lens for every design review
Security: least privilege, encryption everywhere, detective controls — the pillar that constrains the others
Reliability: automatic recovery, horizontal scaling, stop guessing capacity — design for failure, not against it
Cost Optimization: right-sizing, elasticity, pay for value — the pillar that funds the others
Use it as a review ritual: run new architectures through the pillars before building — the review is free, the rework is not

example.code:
# Design review checklist (15 min):
# Security:      least privilege? encrypted? logged?
# Reliability:   multi-AZ? auto-recovery? tested failover?
# Performance:   right type? cached? scaling policy?
# Cost:          right-sized? committed? lifecycle policies?
# Ops Excellence: runbooks? alarms with actions? IaC?
# Sustainability: right region? idle resources off?
# If a pillar has no answer, the design is not done.
example.walkthrough: The checklist turns six abstract pillars into fifteen minutes of concrete questions. Run it before building: a missing answer is a design gap found for free. The exam maps scenarios to pillars — 'cheapest' is Cost Optimization, 'survives failure' is Reliability, 'least access' is Security.

pitfalls: Treating it as exam trivia — it is a design tool; use it on real architectures
Optimizing one pillar blindly — cheapest (cost) vs survives (reliability) is a trade-off to decide, not a default
No review ritual — architectures drift; review at design time and annually
lessons.try_it: Run one of your architectures through the six pillars and write the gaps found.

lessons.title: High Availability and Fault Tolerance
concepts: HA: the system stays up — multi-AZ deploys, load balancers, auto-recovery; fault tolerance: it keeps working through failures
Design for AZ failure: spread across 3 AZs, stateless compute, data replicated — one AZ loss is a non-event
Health checks + Auto Scaling: unhealthy instances replaced automatically — recovery without humans
Loose coupling: queues between tiers — if the worker tier dies, the queue holds the work; nothing is lost
Test it: game days and AZ-failure drills — untested HA is a hope, not a design

example.code:
# HA pattern: ALB -> ASG (3 AZs) -> RDS Multi-AZ
# - ALB health checks route around bad instances
# - ASG replaces failed instances automatically
# - RDS fails over to standby in ~1-2 min
# - SQS between web and workers: worker outage != data loss
# Game day: terminate an AZ's instances, watch recovery.
# RTO measured, not assumed.
example.walkthrough: The pattern stacks the primitives: the ALB routes around failure, the ASG replaces it, RDS fails over, and SQS holds work through worker outages. The game day line is the discipline — terminate instances in one AZ on purpose and measure recovery time. If you have not tested it, you do not have it.

pitfalls: Single-AZ production — one AZ event is a full outage; the exam punishes this
Stateful instances with local data — replacement loses state; stateless compute, state in managed services
HA claimed but never tested — failover that has never fired will surprise you
lessons.try_it: Draw your app's failure domains: what happens when one AZ disappears?

lessons.title: Decoupling with SQS and SNS
concepts: SQS: message queue — producers send, consumers pull at their pace; decouples tiers and absorbs spikes
SNS: pub/sub topics — one message fans out to many subscribers (email, SMS, Lambda, SQS)
Standard vs FIFO: standard is at-least-once and unordered (nearly unlimited throughput); FIFO is ordered, deduplicated, lower throughput
DLQ (dead-letter queue): poison messages go here after max receives — inspect, fix, replay; never lose a message silently
Exam pair: 'decouple components, absorb spikes' is SQS; 'notify many subscribers' is SNS; often SNS -> SQS fan-out

example.code:
# Order pipeline: API -> SNS order-events -> SQS queues
# (fulfillment, email, analytics each get their own queue)
# Consumer: long-poll, process, delete on success.
# Poison message? After 5 receives -> DLQ for inspection.
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders-fulfillment
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders-dlq
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url <fulfillment> \
  --attributes '{"RedrivePolicy":"{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"<dlq>\",\"maxReceiveCount\":5}"}'
example.walkthrough: The fan-out pattern: one SNS publish reaches three queues, each consumed independently — email failures never block fulfillment. The DLQ wiring is the resilience detail: a poison message gets 5 tries, then parks in the DLQ for humans instead of clogging the queue forever. Decouple, absorb, and never silently drop.

pitfalls: No DLQ — poison messages clog the queue and block everything behind them
Standard queue where order matters — payments need FIFO; standard reorders
Synchronous calls between tiers — one slow tier slows everything; queue it
lessons.try_it: Design an order pipeline: API, SNS fan-out, per-consumer queues, DLQs.

lessons.title: Disaster Recovery: RTO and RPO
concepts: RTO: how long until recovered. RPO: how much data you can lose — every DR decision starts here
Backup and restore: cheapest, slowest (hours) — S3/Glacier backups, rebuild on failure
Pilot light: core data replicated, services off — faster (tens of minutes), moderate cost
Warm standby: scaled-down live copy — minutes, higher cost
Multi-site active/active: full traffic everywhere — seconds, highest cost; choose by RTO/RPO, not by ambition

example.code:
# DR ladder (cost ^ as RTO v):
# Backup/restore:  RTO hours,  RPO hours  | $$$ (Glacier backups)
# Pilot light:     RTO ~30min, RPO minutes| $$ (replicated DB, AMIs ready)
# Warm standby:    RTO ~5min,  RPO ~0     | $$$$ (scaled-down live)
# Active/active:   RTO ~0,     RPO ~0     | $$$$$ (full duplicate)
# Pick the cheapest rung that meets the RTO/RPO. Test the failover.
example.walkthrough: The ladder makes DR a shopping decision: read your RTO/RPO, pick the cheapest rung that satisfies them. Most apps land on pilot light or warm standby; active/active is for money-on-the-line seconds. The last line is the rule — an untested DR plan is a document, not a capability.

pitfalls: Active/active for a 4-hour RTO — paying 5x for recovery you do not need
No defined RTO/RPO — the DR discussion never converges without numbers
Untested failover — the runbook works on paper until the region is actually down
lessons.try_it: Write RTO/RPO for your app and pick the cheapest DR rung that meets them.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as Code
concepts: IaC: define infrastructure in code — versioned, reviewed, repeatable; console clicks are not reproducible
CloudFormation: AWS-native — JSON/YAML templates, stacks, change sets (preview before applying), drift detection
Terraform/CDK: multi-cloud or higher-level abstractions — same principle, different tooling
Change sets: preview exactly what a template update will do — the 'plan' before the 'apply'
Exam anchor: 'versioned, repeatable infrastructure' is CloudFormation (or IaC generally); 'preview changes' is change sets

example.code:
# CloudFormation: S3 bucket, versioned and encrypted
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Resources:
  ReportsBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      VersioningConfiguration: {Status: Enabled}
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault: {SSEAlgorithm: 'aws:kms'}
# Deploy: aws cloudformation deploy --template-file s3.yaml --stack-name reports
# Preview: change sets. Drift: detect drift on the stack.
example.walkthrough: The template is eleven lines that replace a console session: versioned in git, reviewed in PRs, deployed identically in every environment. The deploy command creates or updates the stack; change sets preview the diff first; drift detection catches the console-clicker who edited the bucket by hand.

pitfalls: Console-built production — unreproducible, unreviewed, undocumented; template it
Applying template updates blind — change sets exist; preview first
Ignoring drift — manual edits diverge from the template; detect and reconcile
lessons.try_it: Template one existing manual resource in CloudFormation and detect drift on it.

lessons.title: Migration Hub and Discovery
concepts: Migration Hub: the single console tracking migrations across tools — status of every server, database, and app in one place
Application Discovery Service (ADS): agent-based or agentless inventory of on-prem servers — what exists, what talks to what, utilization
Start with discovery, not moving: you cannot plan waves for servers you have not inventoried
Migration Hub Orchestrator: templated workflows (rehost, replatform) — repeatable runbooks for the migration factory
Exam anchor: 'track migration progress centrally' is Migration Hub; 'discover on-prem inventory' is ADS

example.code:
# Discovery first, then track
# 1. ADS agentless discovery via vCenter (or agents on servers)
#    -> inventory: 240 servers, dependencies, CPU/RAM utilization
# 2. Import into Migration Hub -> group into applications
# 3. Orchestrator template: 'rehost' -> automated runbook per wave
# Rule: no server moves before it is discovered, grouped, and waved.
example.walkthrough: The sequence is the methodology: discover (ADS tells you what exists and how it is used), group into applications in Migration Hub, then execute waved runbooks via Orchestrator. Skipping discovery is how migrations miss the database nobody knew about — the most common migration surprise.

pitfalls: Migrating before discovery — the unknown database surfaces mid-cutover
Tracking in spreadsheets — stale the day after creation; Hub is the live view
One big-bang wave — pilot, learn, then factory; waves de-risk
lessons.try_it: Inventory 10 hypothetical servers into applications and assign them to 3 waves.

lessons.title: DMS and Schema Conversion
concepts: DMS: replicate databases with minimal downtime — full load plus ongoing CDC until cutover
Homogeneous (MySQL to MySQL): DMS alone. Heterogeneous (Oracle to Aurora): DMS plus SCT
SCT converts schemas, views, and stored procedures — and reports what cannot convert automatically
Validate before cutover: row counts, checksums, application tests against the replica — cut over on proof, not hope
Cutover pattern: stop writes, let CDC drain to zero lag, flip connection strings, monitor — minutes, not hours

example.code:
# Oracle -> Aurora PostgreSQL, <30 min downtime
# 1. SCT: assess + convert schema (review the action items!)
# 2. DMS task: full-load-and-cdc, source Oracle, target Aurora
# 3. Ongoing: monitor lag (CloudWatch: CDCLatencySource/Target)
# 4. Pre-cutover: row counts + checksums + app smoke tests
# 5. Cutover window: quiesce writes -> lag ~0 -> flip -> monitor
example.walkthrough: The five steps are the runbook: SCT handles what DMS cannot (dialect, procedures), DMS keeps the target current via CDC, validation proves fidelity, and the cutover is a lag-drain plus flip. The CloudWatch lag metrics are the go/no-go signal — cut over when they read near zero.

pitfalls: DMS without SCT for heterogeneous — procedures and schema do not convert themselves
Cutover with lag — writes land on the old database after the flip; drain first
No validation — 'the row counts looked fine' is not validation; checksums are
lessons.try_it: Write the cutover runbook for a MySQL-to-Aurora move: steps, lag thresholds, rollback trigger.

lessons.title: Data Transfer: Online vs Offline
concepts: Online: DataSync for file/object sync (scheduled, verified, throttled); Direct Connect for sustained high throughput
Offline: Snowcone (8TB, edge), Snowball Edge (80TB, compute), Snowmobile (exabytes, truck) — when bandwidth math fails
The math: TB / Mbps = days; if the answer exceeds the deadline, go offline — no tooling beats physics
Transfer Family: SFTP/FTPS/FTP into S3 or EFS — for partners and legacy workflows, not bulk migration
Exam split: 'migrate 50TB with slow uplink' is Snowball; 'ongoing sync' is DataSync; 'partner SFTP' is Transfer Family

example.code:
# Bandwidth math (do this first):
# 50TB at 100 Mbps = ~46 days. Deadline 3 weeks -> Snowball Edge.
# 500GB at 1 Gbps = ~1.2 hours -> DataSync, done today.
# DataSync task: source NFS -> S3, nightly cron, bandwidth limit 200 Mbps
# Snowball: order -> copy at LAN speed -> ship back -> S3 loaded.
example.walkthrough: The math decides before any tooling: compute transfer days from size and uplink, compare to the deadline. DataSync is the managed online mover with scheduling and verification; Snowball moves the bottleneck to LAN-plus-shipping. Transfer Family is the odd one out — a protocol service for ongoing feeds, not migration.
